subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the further consideration of the financial statement which was presented to the House this year it seems unnecessary to quote many figures. Already figures have been quoted at great length, and various hon. members have drawn different conclusions from their reading of the budget speech. To my mind there is nothing in that speech to indicate the hope that the government is taking serious steps to remedy the unemployment situation, to encourage immigration, to reduce expenditures or the public debt, or to reduce the income tax so as to equal the levy in the United States;-this in the face of the fact that nearly all the countries of the world are reducing debt and taxation. I think the. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in presenting the budget showed too much anxiety to declare a surplus. In his claim of five million odd surplus he included a four million dollar item of so-called revenue from Greek and Roumanian loans. He states that he has not received the cash but simply a virtual promise to pay. He had that assurance before. He says, "Our creditors give, as additional security certain of the revenues of these countries as guarantee." Do Greece and Roumania give Canada the right of entry? Or do they give the government the right to place an official in their customs houses charged with the duty of collecting the assured amounts? I do not see that they do. The matter stands just where it did before. The governments of these countries are responsible only in the same degree as before, and in my opinion will honour the obligation because it is an obligation and not because of any material change of record during the past year. These interest arrears can be credited to revenue account only when paid, and have no place in the calculation of a surplus. The additional interest accrued may be an asset, but it is certainly not an item of revenue for the year. As we stand to-day it would seem that if cash loans to the

The Budget-Mr. White
railways and to the merchant marine are considered-and they should be considered-we have a deficit of sixteen or seventeen millions, and if government-guaranteed 'loans to the railways are considered-and in the present condition of the National Railways I do not know of any reason why they should not he considered-we have a deficit of some sixty-four millions more, making something like a total of a hundred millions deficit for this year. I would refer the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in this House in 1923, when he explained the position clearly. He was not afraid to refer to the facts of the railway situation, and he was not afraid of the word "deficit," nor was he afraid finally to make a frank statement to the House as to what the deficit was, after expenses were considered, including the railway and the merchant marine situation.

speechtext:
I think it is to be regretted
that the government did not produce a financial statement which could be understood by the people. Many members of this House, with all their advantages of securing information, have expressed their confusion and dissatisfaction with the statements which are partial and very much beclouded1 in their form of presentation. If the members of this House cannot arrive at a fair estimate of the position of the country how can the people who have not the advantage of a knowledge of the facts arrive at any fair statement of where we stand? We might take, for example, a departmental store or a business house having many departments. In the head office bookkeeping each department is charged with expenditure and credited with revenue derived from thfft department. Would it be reasonable for a great business house or firm, in making up its annual report and budget, to disregard one department which has not been a source of revenue but rather a cause of loss? A statement of that kind placed before a board of directors would not be a correct one, and would hardly be looked on as an honest statement of the year's business. That is the position in which Canada finds herself to-day. The
budget is delivered, a surplus is claimed without taking into consideration the Department of Railways. The claim of surplus or otherwise should be based on the entire business of the year, so that the Canadian people can understand the situation. If the National railways had overnight a year ago reached a position where they not only could take care of operating expenses but also received enough for fixed charges and a surplus besides, I wonder what the Finance Minister would do regarding that surplus. I think it would not be necessary to argue as to the propriety of including the result in the national statement.
This year there are to be some changes in the tariff, in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister announced in Toronto that there would be no tinkering ;n regard to the tariff this year, but that he would wait and see how last year's changes worked out. In 1924 there were thirty-seven changes in the tariff schedule, this year up to date there are sixteen, and the Prime Minister has announced that there may be other changes when the trade agreement with Australia is under consideration.
I have referred on other occasions in this House to the situation so far as the iron and steel industry is concerned, and half of the items changed in the tariff schedule this year affect that industry adversely. The principal items in the budget which affect it are: the increased duties on coal, which I will refer to later; the replacing of certain products on the free list; and the changing back of the item of rolling mill rolls which was put on the free list last year to the former duty of 274 per cent;-during recess this last-named change was made by order in council; the concession, I understand, was made to the iron and steel industry on account of the reduction in duty on its products made last year. If the industry needed that help last September or October, it surely needs it now, and yet the minister says that it has since been represented! to the (government that these rolls are made in Canada. On that account it is proposed to repeal this order in council- and place the rolls back at the former rate of duty. The rolls are manufactured in Canada, but there is no Canadian concern making a specialty of that line of work, and the Canadian roll is inferior to that of American manufacture, not because the Canadian manufacturers are not as skilful as the American manufacturers, but because there is not sufficient market in this country to develop the business and to warrant a foundry making a specialty of that class of work and nothing else. It was represented
The Budget-Mr. White

to the government that rolls were manufactured in Canada, and therefore it was necessary to place them back in the 27 i per cent schedule. It surely was possible for the government in 1924 when they put so much of iron and steel on the free list, to find out that pig iron and bar iron and1 steel were made in Canada. Therefore why should rolls be placed back in the dutiable list and the pig-iron and bars provided for in last year's budget remain on the free list? In addition to that, by the present budget farm and log-' ging sleighs are placed in tariff item 591. That automatically puts the iron and steel bars used in their construction on the free list, and (the Acting Minister of Finance knows now that such goods are made in Canada. There is no other line of business in Canada which has been persecuted to such an extent as the iron and steel business has in the last few years. In the items in the customs tariff to-day, dealing with iron and steel, there are seventeen on the free list. Fourteen of them are subject to 99 per cent drawback; three others in varying amounts from 30 to 80 per cent drawback, which means that practically 32 items are on the free list, and there are only 18 items on which duty is levied. Taking into consideration the British preference and the dumping clause, there is an average duty of less than seven per cent on iron and steel rolling mill products which are on the dutiable list. By the changes in the tariff this year the industry is taxed 27^ per cent on its rolls and 23 to 40 per cent on its coal, and there also exists in other items, duties on machinery and1 supplies, 25 per cent to 30 per cent, and sales tax of 5 per cent on all materials excluding fuel. How can the government expect that industry or any other industry to flourish under such circumstances? In the eleven months ended February 28 of this year, we imported of iron and its products, $118,000,000 worth, $100,000,000 worth of which came from the United States, and our exports to the Unite ! States were a little less than $4,500,000. I would call attention of the House to an Associated Press despatch in the Globe of March 28 in reference to the exportation of pig iron from Ontario to the United States. The despatch reads:
Washington, March 27.-Anti dumping provisions of the Tariff Act were applied to-day by the treasury against the importation of pig iron from the province of Ontario.
While there was no official explanation of the action, it was understood that investigations preceding the order had shown that Ontario manufacturers were able, to sell in territory contiguous to the Great Lakes on

the south, at lower prices because of the cheaper transportation by water. Domestic producers serving the same region, it was stated, must meet that competition after paying freight charges by rail which added materially to the cost to purchasers.
It seems that Uncle Sam's idea of "balance of trade" is to prevent any importation of manufactured goods into the United States and to send out as much as possible to Canadian users, even to the extent, as in the steel business, of $100,000,000 per annum without allowing a ton to go into the United States, if it can possibly be excluded.
That is only one instance in which the government of the United States has acted in the same way. I can cite another of a firm with head office in Toronto, making special building brick, who were recently developing a good trade in the American lake coast cities. The matter was brought to the attention of the American treasury, the tariff was adjusted and increased; so that the exportation of brick from Ontario ceased immediately.
On the tariff the government has surely boxed the compass. When the Liberal party took office in the fall of 1921, the possibility, or the probability, of the adoption of the Liberal platform was the cause of a great deal of speculation. The sessions of 1922 and 1923 saw some small downward changes in the tariff and some compensating changes in the sales tax. A duty was imposed on artificial silk and bounties were provided on the production of copper bars and on binder twine manufactured from hemp grown in Canada. Thus encouragement was held out to three different lines of industry. In 1924, the abolition of the sales tax and the reduction in the duty of agricultural implements and on the materials entering therein, were the features. No encouragement for manufacturers was voiced in the budget speech delivered in that year by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). This year the minister proceeds on another tack. On the one hand he increases the duty on slack coal in an endeavour to encourage coal mining, particularly in Nova Scotia, I imagine, and on the other, he gives the iron and steel industry further discouragement and dismay. This is done by the increased duty on coal, the addition of more iron and steel products to the free list, and the withdrawal of the concession made last year regarding the duty on rolls used in the industry. That is the government's record. There is also the government's record with reference to the five per cent feature in the dumping clause. This was suspended in the early days of the 1924 session, and a few weeks afterwards, according to the words of the Minister of Customs and

The Budget-Mr. White
Excise (Mr. Bureau), "the government had decided to suspend the suspension." In this year's budget, another feeble effort is made to amend the same clause, followed by an announcement a few days later by the Acting Minister of Finance that, "after further consultation with officers of the department, it had been decided that the amending resolution would be withdrawn." In that respect the matter stands in about the same condition as the question in regard to land which the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Kellner) was complaining about a few minutes ago.
The increased duty on slack coal affects not only the iron and steel industry, but many other lines of industry in Quebec and Ontario. This change in the duty on coal was made without any compensating changes being made in other tariff items to offset increased costs of manufacture in other lines of industry. I contend that this matter should have received a comprehensive study before any items were changed, as by changes being made in a few schedules, other items are thrown out of balance and the net result may be the relief of one hardship, only to increase it in another place or in some other line of industry.
Referring to the question of coal particularly, I have no desire to criticize an increase in the duty on slack coal, if the minister, after careful and exhaustive inquiry, satisfies himself and this House that it is necessary for the development of Canadian industry and the well-being of the Canadian people. The average price of bituminous coal, that is, run of mine and lump, at United States mines is to-day about $2.15 a ton. The duty on this coal is reduced 3 cents a ton and stands to-day at 50 cents. This duty reduced to percentage terms on the value of coal is 23| per cent. Slack coal is worth to-day from 90 cents to $1.60 per ton at the mines or an average of $1.25 per ton. The 50 cents per ton duty now levied is a duty of 40 per cent. The hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte) undertook to prove to this House a few evenings ago that that duty was about 13.77 per cent. He chose to go back to the year 1923 for his value of coal, and he took the duty of 1925 and arrived at those figures. If he wanted to make a really nice showing, favourable to his argument, he might have gone back two or three years more and taken the figures when coal was selling at $16 or $18 a ton. That would have made a very low duty; but Canadian users are face to face with the fact that they have to pay a duty of 50 cents a ton on dlack coal which is worth $1.25 a ton, and no amount of figuring
will get away from the fact that that duty is 40 per cent.
Some hon. members of both the Progressive and Liberal parties are wont to rail at the Conservative party as the party of protection, and some even say the party of high protection, but I never heard even the most enthusiastic Conservative advocate a duty of 40 per cent on coal. What party is it which now assumes the role of high protectionists? It is the Liberal party, the party which was to inaugurate a revision downward in the tariff, as the legend runs:	"In order to diminish
the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the great masses of the consuming public of Canada." Yes, they are lightening the burden by collecting, according to the minister's own estimate, just $1,000,000 more in customs duties in the coming year.
What is to be gained 'by this increase of duty? As regards the mines in Nova Scotia, and possibly Alberta, I think the gain is problematical in view of the reported move by the United States railroads to lower freight rates 36 cents a ton to points at which United States slack coal and Nova Scotia coal compete. If the railroad rates are lowered sufficiently to take care of the 36-cent increase in duty, the additional amount of Canadian coal solid will be small. As the business is now conducted, df freights are reduced, the coal will cost about the same at competitive points in the Montreal district, and it will cost users of slack coal further east in Quebec and the Maritimes and further west in Ontario, 36 cents per ton more as there will be no incentive to American railroads to lower freight costs, particularly to Ontario points. By the changes in coal duties, the Minister has placed a levy of 50 cents on an importation worth on an average $1.25, and the same duty on another importation of a value of $2.15. If it was absolutely necessary to make changes in the coal duties, in my vaew it would have been more just to discontinue the specific duties and levy an equitable ad valorem rate.
There is another item in the tariff changes dealing with bituminous coal, calculated to stimulate the production of coke by the use of by-product coke ovens. This item provides for 99 per cent drawback of duty under certain conditions, the idea being, I presume, to make coke in order to have that commodity take the place of anthracite coal. That wiil be of some benefit in so far as it promotes Canadian industry, and the employment of Canadians in the establishment of coking plants, and in the work of producing a material which will make us in some degree more independent of the American anthracite producer.
The Budget-Mr. White

The Budget-Mr. White

1924, will show; and it was not until December, 1924, that any further reductions in prices were made.
I am going to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to help me to prove this contention. In his speech on the Address on February 9, to show what great things had been done for the farmers, he gave what he called a representative list of implements which had been sold in Ontario before the budget of 1924 for the sum of $953.50 and, after the date of the budget, for $905.50. If the farmer had received the full benefit of the reductions of last year's budget, he would have been called upon to pay just $859.55; actually paid $905.50. That is to say, he did not receive the advantage due on account of the reductions of sales tax and duty, by $45.45. The Prime Minister also referred to a slightly larger list sold in the Regina territory before the budget of 1924 for the sum of $1,358 and after the date of the budget for $1,291. In the second instance, if the farmer had received the full benefit of the reduction, the price would have been $1,224.18. In other words, on the western list he did not receive the advantage due on account of the reduction of sales tax and tariff, by $66.82. In fact, in both these cases cited by the Prime Minister the farmer received just about one-half the advantage of the reduction in sales tax and duty. If the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) will make close inquiry he may find that there was a reduction on implements in the United States last year which was largely the compelling reason for the change in prices in December, 1924.
I am not criticizing the manufacturers of agricultural implements in respect to the conduct of their business. Their balance sheets for the last few years would indicate that they are in need of all they are receiving. So far as this budget is concerned, I am criticizing the action of the government in exposing the manufacturers and the workmen of this country to ruinous outside competition.
Another matter referred to in the budget speech of the Acting Minister of Finance was that of an export duty on electric energy. He announced that an order in council had been passed levying an export duty on electric energy which, according to his estimate, will produce a revenue of $400,000 per year. The matter of the principle of power exportation has been pretty fairly discussed, and I need not go into it at any very great 
length. In my own city the consumption has increased by leaps and bounds. Out of a population of about 63,000 the HydroElectric system is supported by 17,500 consumers, 4,200 of whom have electric stoves. Although the city contracted with the commission originally for 3,000 horse-power, the demand to-day is for around 17,000 or 18,000 horse-power and is still increasing. This is typical of the demand wherever electric current is available at low rates, and the prediction is made by hydro engineers that there will be a severe power shortage in two years' time.
I look on the exportation of power as the exportation of another of our raw materials, and I am opposed to a further enlargement of our exports of unmanufactured goods. If we could export it in the form of manufactured goodte made from the application of this power, or if we used it to manufacture many of the goods we now import, I think it would be of infinitely greater benefit to Canada.
As to the exportation now going on, for the year ending March 31, 1924, there were ten companies exporting current, six of whom exported less than 9,000 horse-power from various parts of the country. There is an exportation of about 65,000 horse-power from the Cedar Rapids plant of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company; I have no information about the contracts under which this exportation is made. The balance of our exports, 'about 140,000 horse-power, are from the Niagara district.
In the year ending March 31, 1924, there was exported by the Canadian Niagara Power Company some 53,000 horse-power; by the Toronto Power Company some 34,000 horsepower; and by the Ontario Power Company some 52,000' horse-power. The last two mentioned are Ontario Hydto Commission activities. It has been announced in the press that the contract which the Canadian Niagara Power Company has with the United States consumers provides that any duties imposed by the government shall be paid by the consumer. If that is the case it definitely fixes the payment on the United States consumer. Now, the contract of the Toronto Power Company also has the same clause fixing the duty on the consumer, and I am informed that this contract was for a five-year period, expiring on October 25 of this year.
The contract in the name of the Ontario Power Company is for exportation to the Niagara-Lockport Company and was signed in 1903, three years before the passing of the act to regulate the exportation of electric power.

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
The contract originally called for the exportation of 60,000 horse-power, and under certain options might not expire until the year 2010. When the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario purchased the Ontario Power Company in 1917 the terms of the contract with the Niagara Loekport Company ware changed, so that the present contract expires in 1950.
The Dominion charter granted the Ontario Power Company in 1887 gives the Power Company the right to export power to the United States and makes no mention of the addition of a tax by the government. I am informed that the contract with the American company does not provide for the payment of any taxes. This long term contract is for' power at an extremely low rate and will mean probably a loss to the Hydro Commission of Ontario. On the basis of last year's exportation of 52,000 horse-power, the export duty would amount to $101,400 per year. If they export the full 60,000 horse-power of the contract the duty will amount to $117,000 per year. Now if the Hydro-Electric Commission is taxed to this amount, and is unable to collect from the American consumer, who pays the tax? It will be charged to the Niagara system of the commission's activities, and that charge will have to be met by those who are using current from that system. The reports of the commission show that 54 per cent of their revenue is derived from the sale of energy for commercial light and power and the balance of 46 per cent comes from the use by public utilities and domestic services, the domestic services being about two-thirds of the 46 per cent. Thus in the final analysis so far as this $117,000 per year is concerned the people of Ontario who are using Niagara energy will pay the tax.
This is only another practical illustration of the way the government is reducing the "very high cost of living which presses so severely on the people." Now I make these suggestions to the government; that the order in council be amended to provide that, if, in the case of an export contract, existing prior to the passing of the order in council, the duty cannot be collected from the American consumer, that contract shall be exempted from the duty. That the government revoke all export licenses as the existing contracts expire. While I am strongly in favour of curtailing export, if, under special circumstances it is deemed wise to issue any further licenses, I suggest they be for short terms only.
Considering the budget as a whole, if we judge by the contradictory opinions expressed by the members of the Liberal party, it is 145i
evident that the government is unable to advance a policy which meets the needs of the country, whether on account of these internal divergencies of view of the party or the fear of defeat in the House, I am unable to determine; but it seems to me that there is a worse fate than defeat in the House, and that is a loss of the confidence of the people. I believe the government by its vacillations has forfeited the confidence of the Canadian people and deserves the censure of this House.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to all that has been said in this debate, but I must say that I find myself unable to agree with all of it; because I think the compass has been pretty well boxed, the wind has blown from nearly every direction, and therefore it would be impossible to agree with all that has been said. I might preface my remarks with the words of the old sailor who, when he was in danger, said, "Oh, Lord, I aint one of them chaps as is always bothering you, I don't often do it, I aint ever done it before, and if you listen to me this once it may be some time before I do it again." This debate, as I say, has been very varied, it has led us all over the country and treated of different periods of our history. I have endeavoured to take a calm, judicial and impartial view of the debate, and on the whole I think that the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is to be congratulated on the budget which he has presented to the House and to the country. I remember very well some three months ago when our newspapers were full of rumours of the large deficit that might be expected. It was said that the customs revenue and the income tax had fallen off, and before the House met it was considered almost inevitable that the Acting Minister of Finance would have to provide for a large deficit. However, we had the satisfaction of hearing him announce a surplus-a surplus of $2,000,000 considered in one way, and of some $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 considered in another way. ,
I am one of those, Mr. Speaker, who thinks that on the whole the budget is a fair presentation of the country's position. I say so for various reasons:	First, as far as I can
exercise my judgment on it; second, because I have a high degree of confidence in the honesty and integrity of the Acting Minister of Finance, whose record both in his public and in his private life is such that it will put to shame some of those members who have seen fit in this House to cast aspersions upon him; another reason that leads me to the con-
The Budget-Mr. Raymond

elusion that is now firmly in my mindi is the argument of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). He is an authority in this House on matters of finance, he is the ex-Minister of Finance, and consequently I listened to his argument with a great deal of attention. But there was one aspect of the debate that I thought deplorable; I could not apply any other word to it. The honour and dignity of this House, Mr. Speaker, is something which we all should do our best to preserve, and in view of the fact that it was hon. gentlemen opposite who constituted themselves the guardians of our honour and dignity, those hon. gentlemen have to my mind somewhat grievously trespassed upon it this session. I mean, for instance, that when the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) in referring to the Acting Minister of Finance, said that the system of bookkeeping he had employed to arrive at the conclusion he did in his budget was such as men were "doing time"-I believe that was his expression-for having used. Now, I think such expressions are to be deplored. I thought that this particular expression would have constituted a breach of ,the rules of this House, but I suppose it was taken as many another word from that hon. member is taken, as a joke, a friendly utterance, for he is fond of making jocular remarks. But I think this remark was too serious almost to be taken jocularly. Besides, ,when statements are made in this House they are not made to the limited circle that listen to them here. An instance of that happened just the other day, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) found himself reported in the Chicago Tribune as having been in this House almost a champion of annexation and as having stated that one-third of our population were in favour of annexation. He was surprised himself when he saw the report. Now, supposing some member of a foreign country, or the representative of a foreign newspaper, were in the gallery at that time and heard the ex-Minister of Finance state that for methods of bookkeeping the same as were used by the Acting Minister of Finance people were "doing time," would not he be warranted in going .back to his own country and saying that when he was in the legislature of Canada he heard a man of experience, a man of repute, rise and state that its membership was composed of men who were no better than felons and convicts?
I speak with all respect, and all earnestness and I say that I deplore such an act. I think it is to be regretted, and I should like to see the hon. member for West York (Sir
	'
Henry Drayton) withdraw those words. I do not know whether he said them in earnest, or as a bit of a joke as he does sometimes. But when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) hurled such a frightful phrase across the floor as "moral obloquy" I felt certain, Mr. Speaker, it Was more or less harmless because nobody has ever seen the words herded together in just that shape before, and most of the House had a doubt as to whether the hon. member himself was really aware of the meaning of the words he was using, because we know that " obloquy " if it is taken in the sense of " abuse, detraction and disparagement " does not belong to the side of the House on which the Acting Minister of Finance is sitting; it belongs to the far corner of the House to your left Mr. Speaker. That is where "abuse, detraction and disparagement," which are given in the dictionary as the meaning of the dreadful word which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre used, come from; that is the comer of the House where such expressions emanate; that is the comer of the House where the three more prominent members I have referred to sit as the premier scholars in the school of scolds. They have copied-^with a degree of fidelity which would be admirable if it were for a better purpose-the manner of their great teacher, but they have been unable to appropriate or imitate bis attainments or his talents.
Now, I wish to show you, Mr. Speaker, and show the House, how it is that the hon. member for West York has induced me to think that this may be a very good and very sound budget. As I say, I take that view partly from my own examination of the figures, and partly also because of the high reputation of the hon. gentleman; but now I wish to confine myself more particularly to tfie slant that was given to my mind1 by the arguments of the hon. member for West York when the statement was made that the surplus did not exist, and when he attempted to prove that not only did the surplus not exist but that many of the items that were referred to could not possibly be applied to the account. He went on to add certain other items to the liabilities until he proved, entirely to his own satisfaction, that instead of a surplus there existed a deficit of some SI 10,000,000. I followed that argument with much interest because, as I say, he is a gentleman of very high financial repute; he not only knows all about [DOT] railways and shipping but he also knows all about finance, and some of his ardent admirers say that he even understands law-of course, to

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
a certain extent. But, Mr. Speaker, when, as I say, a gentleman of that high repute and that knowledge, and in whose judgment I have so much confidence, proved absolutely that there was a deficit of $110,000,000 I had, of course, to conclude that those were not the words of a mere-shall I say?-hon. member, not the words of a politician, but the words of a great statesman, the words of one to whom had been entrusted the financial management of this country, one who had been entrusted with its financial management just prior to the accession of the present government, mark you. He proved there was a deficit of $110,000,000 instead of their being a surplus of $2,000,000. That was the effect of his argument. And then we had the interesting spectacle of the way in which the statesman would remedy the deficit of $110,000.000. In order to meet that deficit what does he suggest? They say, Mr. Speaker, that "actions speak louder than words." Now, the hon. member's action was embodied in his amendment in which he says that the taxes should be still further reduced. What effect would that have? According to his amendment he would meet the deficit of $110,000,000, which he says exists, by still further reducing the sales tax, the stamp tax, the income tax, and other taxes by which revenue has been raised for a number of years back. Well, I could not imagine any spectacle much more ridiculous offered by a gentleman who claimed to have balanced the affairs of this country than in him to rise in this House and prove that there is a much greater deficit than the Acting Minister of Finance says, and yet to be so satisfied that it does not exist that he is willing to vote for a further reduction of taxes; whereas if he knew that a deficit of $110,000,000 existed the taxes would have to be increased in order to meet it. I say I cannot imagine a much more ludicrous spectacle unless the proposition was advanced as another of those little jokes which we have from my hon. friend from time to time and which we are always glad to have, because there is not a merrier sound in this House than the laugh of the hon. gentleman.
Following up the argument contained1 in the hon. member's speech, in addition to discovering a deficit of $110,000,000 and evincing a desire to still further reduce the taxes of the country, what does the hon. member propose further? He proposed in the course of his speech to keep out of this country some $700,000,000'-I think that was the amount- on raw materials, and so forth, which arc imported into the country and upon which
duty is paid, thus proposing to take away another $100,000,000 from our revenue. That was his proposition-that the tariff should be raised to keep those raw materials out. Tnat is to say no tariff would1 be derived from their importation, and another $100,000,000, or in that vicinity, would be added to the existing deficit of $110,000,000. That is the way in which my hon. friend would meet deficits. Is it any wonder that when the affairs of this country were in the hands of a gentleman whose mathematics would lead him in this peculiar direction, that when he left office we should find a huge debt of $2,500,000,000 upon this country? To me it is not in the least surprising. But it was somewhat surprising when the hon. member for London (Mr. White) followed in the same strain. These gentlemen must understand that if the deficit they speak of really exists it is impossible to carry out the amendment for which, I expect, the hon. member for London and others will vote-to still further reduce the taxes. On the other hand if we have such a deficit the thing necessary for us to do, it seems to me, is to raise enough taxes. We know that should be the course to meet such a deficit if it really existed, and the hon, member for West York knows it also. But the hon. member probably does not think it really does exist because, as I say, his remarks were simply uttered in that very pleasant spirit of jocularity which we all enjoy and which amuses us so much.
Now, with regard to the tariff itself there are just one or two items that I wish to allude to because they affect my own constituency. It is rather difficult to touch the tariff, Mr. Speaker, without affecting the constituency of Brantford because, as I stated before in this House, and which is known to most members, its manufactures go all over Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. When a reduction was made in the duty on the articles manufactured there last year I was in hopes nothing more would be touched; I was in hopes that we would stand pat upon the budget-although that does not seem to please hon. gentlemen straight across the chamber; I hoped that the tariff would remain with some degree of steadiness for a few years until such changes as had been brought in by the budget of last year might have had a chance to work and enable us to see whether they would be a benefit. However, a further reduction is made this year on farm wagons and farm sleighs. The duty has been reduced, I think, from some-
The Budget-Mr. Raymond

thing like 25 per cent to something like 10 per cent. This reduction affects another Brantford industry-because not only did the wagons of the Adams Wagon Works carry the food of our gallant soldiers over the blood-soaked fields of France and Flanders, but they are used on farms in our own country in a peaceful way in a territory extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Now this further reduction was made.
Was there one word of appreciation for the further reduction from the members of the Progressive party? If there was I failed to hear it. I heard most of what was said. I heard them complain that the budget did not suit them. They did1 not point out that this particular item did not suit them, and they did not point out that this item was adjusted for their benefit and in their interest. The thought that is in my mind at the present time, that was in my mind last year was this- and I am quite in earnest when I say it, and I hope that no offence will be taken for I intend none-that whatever reductions are made in the budget, whatever changes are made for the benefit of the Progressives, they will never be satisfied, they will ask for more, and will not wait to see how the changes made last year benefit them. But there comes this insistent demand for further reductions every session, and it reminds me of the story of the bear and the boy with the candy. The bear will eat the candy as long as the boy has the candy and will give it to him; then when the candy is gone the bear will eat the boy. That is the attitude of the Progressive party on the tariff, and I regret to say it. I do not wish to offend any member of that party, but I would like to see them come to a more reasonable attitude upon this question. Of course there are some questions which we naturally view from different angles. They are consumers and users of these goods that are made so largely in the city I represent, but it is their uncompromising attitude I complain of. They never seem satisfied. As I have stated, I have not heard one word uttered from that corner of the House complimenting the government or the Acting Minister of Finance on this very change in respect to the duty on wagons which was made for their benefit. That is a large and important industry in Brantford, and will be affected very seriously by the change. The firms in the western states that make wagons which go to the northwest are situated much closer to the people of the prairie provinces than we are- a good many hundred miles. Their freight rates are less, and consequently it will be very difficult for the manufacturer in Brant-

ford to compete with the American wagon makers andl keep their trade. Yet it is known that there is no better article of that class manufactured anywhere in Canada. It can only be put out of the market by a lower price, with the advantage in the freight rates that American manufacturers will have. These wagons are largely made in the vicinity of Minneapolis and that would make it very difficult for the Adams Wagon Works for instance to continue to compete against them.
This brings me to another point which I desire to touch briefly, which is not directly referred to in the budget, and I regret that it has not been mentioned. I think it should have been mentioned in some way. I refeT to the Crowsnest pass agreement which has created discrepancies and discriminations against many points throughout the whole of Canada, but I venture to say that no point has suffered more on account of the inequalities in the freight rates than the city of Brantford. Our complaint is not simply that the discrimination was put into effect by the Canadian Pacific Railway, 'because that is not the main railway serving the city. It is one of them, but not the principal one. Our complaint is that the Canadian National Railway should have granted a rate to the city of Hamilton which is discriminatory against the city of Brantford, and rival manufactories are located in the city of Hamilton. In order to give hon. members some idea of the enormous difference that this makes on some classes of agricultural implements that are shipped to the northwest, Brantford has to pay a rate of $1.28 per hundred, while the same goods are carried at the rate of 96 cents a hundred from Hamilton, and these goods are carried, not by a rival railway, but by our own Canadian National. That discrimination against the city of Brantford has been put into effect by the Canadian National Railways. Of course the excuse is that when the Crowsnest pass agreement came into effect and the Canadian Pacific Railway gave reduced rates from Hamilton, the Canadian National had to grant a reduced rate to meet it. Whatever excuse may be offered by the Canadian National Railways or by its officials, the feeling naturally will exist, and it will rankle in the hearts of shippers by railway in Brantford that this discrimination is made against them by the Canadian National Railways. The feeling in our district was growing greatly in favour of the Canadian National, and there was a desire to ship goods by that road. The railway had come into favour and was found to be giving

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
good service. People were satisfied with it and became proud of it. But there is a strong feeling there to-day, and they want to know why should the Canadian National Railways, discriminate against them when they are shipping their most important product to the west. Why should they have to pay $1.28 per hundred, when the same goods could be shipped from the city of Hamilton at 96 cents per hundred? In the case of the shipment of some agricultural implements it makes a difference of more than one hundred dollars a car. I think this state of affairs should be rectified, and the Minister of Railways should do something to provide a remedy.

speechtext: I am trying, Mr. Speaker, to get from the hon. member a statement of the facts which are important, because we in the west are much concerned in this proposition. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will answer my hon.
friend's question at a little greater length and explain the argument from the Brantford point of view. I am speaking now trom my own knowledge of it, because I happened to be there when the first connection was put through which gave us any communication at all with the Canadian Pacific Railway, or which gave Hamilton any connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, so far as my knowledge will carry me. The point I wish to make has not been developed at all. The Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo railway was built from Toronto to Hamilton, I think, about 1895, at all events before the Crownest pass rates came in. I say that it is through the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway that the Canadian Pacific Railway came to have any connection with the city of Hamilton. They had running rights at this time which they had arranged for with the Grand Trunk between Hamilton and Toronto. They never built a line from Toronto to Hamilton, but obtained running rights over the then Grand Trunk from Toronto to Hamilton. The city of Brantford withheld the bonus from the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway because they had not carried out the agreement which had been made to build a line from Toronto to Hamilton. That is the connection between the city of Hamilton and the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway as I see it. If that is the connection then the city of Brantford is just as much entitled to the Crowsnest rates as ever the city of Hamilton was. Another contention I make is that whatever the Canadian Pacific Railway have done, if the Canadian Pacific Railway gave an unjust rate from Hamilton to the detriment and disparagement of Brantford and the business there, I do not think it is any excuse for the Canadian National Railways,
The Budget-Mr. Raymond

our own national railway, to give a rate that discriminates against that city. If the Canadian National gave the rate in Brantford, the Canadian Pacific would have to come down and give the same Tate, as now the Canadian National say that they have to give this rate in Hamilton because the Canadian Pacific gave it. I do not know that it is worth while to go into this at any greater length, but it seems to me it is very plain that Brantford is being discriminated against. Section 55 of the Railway Act states that there shall be no discrimination; but in violation of that section our own railroad has given this discrimination against Brantford that some of our cars have to pay $100 more in freight than cars going from Hamilton, and on many other goods the difference is something like 34 per cent more if sent from Brantford than if sent from Hamilton, because the difference is 'between 96 cents and $1.28. I should like to see this rectified.	It was
promised in the Speech from the Throne that transportation would take up the attention ,of the government during this session, and it has been promised by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), who I know is a man who always keeps his promises, that this will be rectified. But months are going by and this is the time of year when vast quantities of agricultural implements are being shipped out. It will soon be the time of year when tons and tons of binder twine will be shipped out, and all these goods have to pay this excessive rate, which I claim is unjust. It is, therefore, the duty of the government and the Canadian National Railways to rectify this and to see that the disparagement against Brantford is done away with.
I was a little disappointed in the amendment that was moved by the hon. member for Brandon, the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke). Perhaps I had allowed my hope to rise a little too easily. When, last year, certain changes were made in the duties on agricultural implements, reducing them, I would say, to an irreducible minimum, I had hoped that these hon. gentlemen would be satisfied. But they were not, and that resolution showed that they were not.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon. member says, "hear, hear". I quite understand' that there are hon. gentlemen over there who will never be satisfied until all the duty is taken off, and I do not know what they will then ask from the government. Their share of the taxes largely consists in the paltry duty they pay on what they use. I should not like to think they pay it grudgingly; I should like to think 	,	:! :|j|U
they pay it cheerfully and with a good heart, because in the amendment that the hon. member for Brandon desired to move, he took the ground that he regretted that the protective principle still1 existed' in the tariff, that is, the extraordinarily high protection of 10 per cent upon ploughs and the extraordinarily high protection of 6 per cent upon binders. I do not know any other country in the world where there is less duty on these goods where any is charged. The hon. member said in his resolution-I will not quote the words of it at length-that they believed rather in the revenue principle than in the protective principle in a tariff. If one wished to collect any revenue, what amount would one impose in duty less than 10 per cent or 6 per cent or the paltry amounts charged on these implements? I cannot conceive it; but I make this suggestion to the Acting Minister of Finance and for anyone who is interested in the finances of this country. If these hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere-and' I do not like to suggest that they are not; it is only that they do not thoroughly understand the matter-in their desire for a revenue tariff, thlat is whiat I have always wanted' and we are quite in accord. Then I understand why it was that the hon. member for East York (Mr. Harris) referred to some hon. members in this House as "Go-on Liberals." That is, according to my understanding, Progressive Liberals. I must be one of those because I believe also in a revenue tariff, but I believe that revenue tariff should be put on a regular and sound basis. More than that, if that was adopted on everything, if it was agreed: that there should be a certain minimum tariff of say-10 per cent on the imports of this country, I would suggest that when the tariff was reduced to that, it should be considered thiat it was reduced1 to the irreducible minimum and that there would be no further reductions. That would be my idea of a minimum tariff. My idea would be to impose that tax on all goods coming into this country unless there was some special reason why a tax ought not to be imposed or unless there was some special reason why a higher tax should be imposed in certain cases.
The hon. member for Brandon said that he regretted the government had not done more to reduce the cost of living. He should have been a little more concrete and definite. How would he proceed to reduce the cost of living? Let us take the items on the cost of living sheet and see which of them are the highest at the present time. You will find such items as butter, milk, cheese, poultry, eggs, meat, bread, all the products of the farm,.

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
are at a higher rate than they usually are on the cost of living sheet. Are those the articles he wants reduced? I do not think he wishes to see any of them reduced. When we know that the few articles of clothes and tea or whatever else we use are not as high, it would have been more interesting, more pointed, if the hon. member had told us on what articles he wanted the tariff reduced in the hope of making the cost of living less.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about automobiles?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know that in
the cost of living automobiles can be considered unless one had to live like a gentleman on a western prairie farm. I do not consider an automobile is an actual necessity of existence, because it is on the artioles that are considered necessary for existence that this table is based every year, as I understand the matter.
Let me continue my serious suggestion and it is this. The hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Thurston), I think, last night suggested that until we reduced the interest on our national debt, we could not hope very much to reduce the annual expenses of this country. We are met every year with a large uncontrollable expenditure, which varies a little, but which runs somewhere about $135,000,000 that we have to pay on our debt. Unless a direct and definite effort is made to reduce that debt it never will be reduced; it will stay about where it is. It is never going to come down until the attention of the people and the government is deliberately set towards reducing it. Do you think it will be reduced, when we have a deficit of $110,000,000, by still further reducing the taxes or by taking away the customs duties on $700,000,000 worth of goods that are imported, as was suggested by the hon. member for West York. (Sir Henry Drayton). That will not reduce the national debt. I should think it was due to his belief in such a course that when he left office he left us with the enormous debt of $2,500,000,000 or whatever it was in his time. The finances of this country should be considered in a serious and direct systematic way. Some system should be evolved as was suggested by the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., whereby we should have something in the nature of a sinking fund or something that would be applied every year towards the reduction of the debt. It need not necessarily be segregated away in a sinking fund, but some definite portion of the revenue of this country should every year be devoted towards the reduction
of the national debt. Until that is done, it will never be [DOT] reduced, and until we reduce our uncontrollable expenses, it will be absolutely impossible for us to get along with less taxation. Therefore, I think that system either of a sinking fund or of apportioning a certain part of the revenue towards the reduction of this vast debt of ours should be put into effect. We could reduce the annual charge on interest and lighten definitely and satisfactorily the burdens of our people. If hon. gentlemen opposite believe, as they say they do, in a revenue tariff, would it not be a good plan to combine the principle of the sinking fund for the reduction of the national debt with the idea of a tariff for revenue?

speechtext:
I understood there was a reduction on farm wagons and sleds; that was the information I got from one company who evidently are under a misapprehension. I hope the hon. gentleman's interpretation of the schedule is correct, because I know that the company do not want to represent the position as it is not. Coming back to the question I was discussing a moment ago, of some gradual, systematic reduction of the national debt, hon. gentlemen opposite claim to be in favour of a revenue tariff, and I say that our revenue will be obtained through the medium of a tariff as long as most of us are alive; and so long as that is the case the main point for us is to see that it is fairly, reasonably, equitably and consistently collected. I think myself that by combining these two ideas, of a reduction of'the national debt, whether in the form of a sinking fund or not, with a revenue tariff, we should obtain satisfactory results; if a certain part of
The Budget-Mr. Raymond

the customs tariff were devoted every year to the reduction of the national debt you would get a proper system by which the tariff would be stabilized.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman in favour of a revenue tariff entirely, or does he look for incidental protection along with it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would be impossible
to have a revenue tariff without giving incidental protection. If for the sake of collecting a revenue we levied a duty of 10 per cent on any particular article, naturally there would be a certain amount of advantage in the way of protection to the implement affected. So that you could hardly separate a certain amount of protection from a revenue tariff. It used to be called "revenue .tariff with incidental protection," but I believe the phrase is a little old now. That was the tariff used more particularly prior to 1011 and 5 p.m. it was fairly successful in Canada, if you will remember. I do not think we have reason to regret that part of our financial history; there was a period of years during which that tariff was in force and I think the business of the country flourished fairly well then. I do not mean to say that this was because of the tariff, but business flourished while that tariff was in existence. To make it a rule that a certain part of the customs tariff should go to the reduction of the national debt would have the effect of stabilizing the tariff, and I feel that it would be quite acceptable to my hon. Progressive friends if they looked at the matter as I do. It would have the advantage of gradually reducing the debt, and further ft would be a means of collecting the money indirectly. I know that some people do not like the term "indirect taxation" and for that reason they object to a tariff. But there will always be some necessity for indirect taxes. And one difference, not the only one of course, between a direct tax, such as the income tax, and an indirect tax by way of a tariff, is that if a man is economically inclined, if he wishes to live, or if being poor he is bound to live, with the greatest amount of frugality, he can avoid using such articles as the duty is collected upon. But if from his salary there is a direct levy in the way of an income tax he cannot practise such economy, and this has a tendency to destroy thrift and frugality. If there were a duty, as we have a duty, on certain articles, those who wished to avoid expense in connection with them could do so by refraining from buying those things. If there .were a duty on tea and they did not w.sh to use tea, or if a tariff were imposed against tobacco and they wanted to economize in that direction, they

could refrain from the use of these commodities. I throw that out seriously as a suggestion; I think that a certain amount of the tariff might be used every year towards the reduction of the national debt; and as our hon. friends opposite believe in a revenue tariff I hope they will give the idea fair consideration. If they do so I flunk they .will agree with me.
Let me say a word now in reference to what has been said regarding the proposed board of tariff commissioners. I think that the hon. member who referred to the matter last night, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Thurston) I believe, icited a strong objection to it, and that was a reason, he said, why we would vote against the budget. I wondered when he said that if he were aware that this board of tariff commissioners will be practically no more than an advisory board of experts to the government. Neither this government nor any other government, nor this nor any other parliament, will ever place in the hands of any commission the power to increase or decrease the tariff as it might see fit, for that would be contrary to the whole theory and genius of our constitution. That of course is not the case in the United States; there the tariff board may put the duties up or down as they please. That could not ibe done in this country, inasmuch as it must rest with parliament to decide what the changes either upward or downward shall be in the duties. If the hon. member, as his remarks implied, was under some misapprehension in this regard, thinking that the matter would be left in the hands of the tariff commission to raise or lower the duties, and if that was what he objected to, I think he need have no fear, because the tariff commission is intended to be merely an extension of the present board that assists the government with advice from outside men who are experts in this matter or who have had business experience in the various questions that come under consideration. Full information upon all these subjects could be laid before the government, and in this way it would come from a free and unbiased source, from the hands of those who are neither prejudiced nor interested. The proper (placing of the tariff is a very delicate matter indeed, and those who have spoken in this House, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), besides several others on the opposite side who followed in the same course, have suggested a reciprocal tariff, a retaliatory tariff similar to that in the United

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
States. Well, such a tariff would not suit us at all; why should we want to imitate the United States? Surely to God we are a country of our own and do not need to copy any other. What we want is a tariff best suited to the needs of Canada, and we should frame such a tariff as the Canadian people themselves want. There are Canadian people who would not like such a tariff as is in force in the United 'States. Suppose for example we had a tariff on woollens, such as there is in the United States, so high that no woollens could be imported from Europe, from Great Britain or anywhere else. Are there not people who would object to that in this country? Yet that is the condition of the tariff in the United States. And would our shoe manufacturers agree to a schedule that levied no duty at all on shoes? But there is no duty on this article in the American tariff. Again, take agricultural implements; agricultural implements in the American tariff are free, and some hon. gentlemen opposite will agree with me that they never want to see these things free in this country. Certainly the city I come from, the constituency I have the honour to represent, would never think it fair, in view of the distance they have to send their goods, to say nothing of some of the disadvantages under which they have to make them, that they should all come in free. But I do not think we could ever expect to have a tariff that would be similar to the United States tariff or the tariff Of any other country; we want to have a tariff of our own that is suited to our own needs. Now, I did not intend to say much about the tariff, but somehow the debates on the budget generally seem to take that angle, and I have ventured to make these few remarks on the subject.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer before I resume my seat. We hear a great many arguments with reference to what would happen to this country if an extremely high tariff, a thoroughly protective tariff, was adopted. As I say, the manufacturers in the city of Brantford are naturally not free traders, and I do not think anyone in this House would accuse me of being a free trader either. But while they are not free traders I do not know that they want a tariff that would, so to speak, reach the sky, the kind1 of tariff that some people have suggested, as high as Haman's gallows. There is a motion on the order paper in the name of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen); I believe it came out in the newspapers even before it appeared on the order paper. It has been referred to in this debate,
and if I am not out of order I should like to refer to it for a moment. He first adverts to the depression that prevails in the country and attributes it to the tariff conditions as they at present exist; then he goes on to state in very glowing terms-it is a beautifully written motion-what benefits would accrue to the country if those conditions were removed. Now, on the very first premise we do not agree with the right hon. gentleman. I do not agree that all the misfortunes of this country, all the depression of business, all the unemployment that exists, come from the tariff. These conditions are found to an even greater extent, as was shown here by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), or at least to as great an extent, in the United States, which is regarded as a highly protected country. When the conditions exist there as they exist here, surely we cannot accept the suggestion that our troubles can be laid at the door of the tariff. I can remember thirty years ago when from 1893 to 1898 we had just as hard times, just as much unemployment, as we have now, though we were then under the old National Policy, which was passed in 1879 and continued from that year until 1897, I believe. There were just as many people out of work, just as many idle factories between 1893 and 1897 as there are to-day, so that I do not think the cause is correctly stated in my right hon. friend's motion.
Now, the results that are supposed to accrue from this imaginary policy-and the policy, mark you, is indicated only in the most general way-are extremely attractive; in fact, alluring -busy factories, happy homes, and all the rest of it. Holding the views that I do with regard to tariff, and coming from an industrial centre, Mr. Speaker, I should look at that suggestion, and I am sure every manufacturer in the city of Brantford would do the same, with a great deal of caution. They would be reminded of those words of Scripture:	"Surely in vain
the net is spread in the sight of any bird.'' Because they remember that the author of that resolution was the one who in 1910 was the first to moot the reduction on agricultural implements and ploughs. They remember that the right hon. leader of the opposition was the one who in 1919 in one fell swoop wiped the duty off farm tractors, of which some $20,000,000 were imported in two years, as a consequence of which the two factories making these articles in Brantford were put out of existence. They remember that he was the author of that; they have not forgotten it, and when they look at that notice of motion they wonder if he will do anything like that again.
The Budget-Mr. Raymond
