subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did not the people of Brantford at the last election vote in favour of the Liberal policy to remove the duty entirely on agricultural implements?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I never knew that it was the policy of the Liberal party to remove the duty entirely, but they voted for me and it was not my policy.
Now, as I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, this is a serious question. To speak of the National Policy is but using vague terms; there is nothing definite about it. Let some definite statement be made as to what will be done before any such motion as is proposed by the leader of the opposition can be accepted by those who do not believe in free 
trade or do not believe in too low a tariff. I say they certainly will never believe in it until they see it more clearly set forth; and why should they? When I came to this House-and this is my fourth session-I was entirely ignorant of all public questions; I came here with a kind1 of ingenuous- guilelessness which caused me to believe that what men said they meant. Now, as I have said, you know, Mr. Speaker, that no one would take me for a free trader; in fact, I have some protectionist proclivities in my cranium. At the first session the tariff as brought down in the budget was not exactly a protectionist tariff or a free-trade tariff. An amendment was moved by the so-called protectionists, the effect of which was that the King government had not carried out its pledges given in 1919. Anyone reading the amendment would say that hon. gentlemen opposite wished to see those pledges carried out. Now, I did not wish to see them carried out, I am free to say.	At the next
session an amendment to the budget was moved, I think, by the hon., member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) the respected leader of the Progressive party. All those gentlemen who had brought in this motion with reference to the pledges of the platform of 1919 turned ini and voted with the Progressive party. Again last year, I cannot remember the exact form of, the amendment, but it was not anything at all that would lead definitely to a protective policy. I stand open to correction if it was. Then take the amendment now before us. It avoids the question absolutely, and it merely speaks for a still further reduction of taxes in order to reduce the deficit of $110,000,000! That is the ridiculous position at the present time-a further reduction of taxes without any reference to protection or to anything else! While this may seem like a joke, to me it is a most serious question. It will stand forever on the records of this House, and cool-brained men will look it over and they will say, "Here was an ex-minister of the crown, one of the greatest financial minds in the country, who when, according' tp his own statement, there was a deficit of $110,000,000, proposed to remedy it by a still further reduction of taxes!" That will stand as long as the records of this House are preserved. There is nothing in this amendment. If the right hon. leader of the opposition were in earnest on this protective policy, and if he wished to get the support of manufacturers, I would expect to see him more definite. The first session I came to this

The Budget-Mr. Morrison
House I expected them to mail their protectionist colours to the mast and fight and die for them. But those colours are nowhere to be seen. We cannot tell how much is meant, or how little is meant, by this amendment. If they mean a reduction of the sales tax and .so forth, if that is the important thing in their mind, how are we to get at their attitude on the tariff? That such a state of uncertainty should exist is not by any accident; it is by design, Sir. The right hon. gentleman knows well the feeling in this country. He has agents from the Atlantic to the Pacific who keep him posted, and he knows just as well as I do that if he came before the country with a policy of high protection he would find that six of the provinces would not send him a single supporter any more than they did in 1921; he would find that in the Maritime provinces, he would find that in the prairie provinces; he would get no supporters there; and he would find that he would not increase his following in Ontario, in Quebec or in British Columbia. He knows this, and that is why, I say, he avoids the question. If I am wrong- which I may be, because I am not infallible -if I am wrong he will have an opportunity to lay before this House definitely in the form of pledges the policy which he intends to pursue. But to carry that policy into effect, if it were ever in the power of any government to do so, I say most solemnly that I believe it would shatter confederation to its original fragments. That is not what we want to see. We want to see the provinces each like a separate little nation, all happy and bound together in the great nationhood of Canada. That is what we have aspirations for. We want Canada to accomplish something in this world. It seems to me that Canada stands for something. There is a kind of genius in the spirit of this country that is illustrated in its history and in the Act of Confederation-it is, Sir, the spirit of conciliation. Before confederation there were warring provinces that were almost at each other's throats, and there was no possible hope of agreement. But first came the spirit of conciliation, then the spirit of compromise, then the spirit of co-operation, and finally confederation. Let us preserve that confederation so established. On the other hand, if, as some say, there is danger of its being wrecked and ruined now, if, as they say, one-third of our population seek annexation, or if there are those at either end of the Dominion who do not believe in confederation, let us set to work at the task anew, let us start a new policy of compromise and co-operation, let us get this country into the proper state
to be a united country. And we must do that if we want to have it become a successful country.
When I say the spirit of conciliation seems indigenous to the country, I think in all its history is no event we have more reason to be proud of than this, that it was on the soil of Canada that the warring English and French were united through the spirit of conciliation, of compromise, that spirit of conciliation and compromise eventuating in confederation, that [DOT] while still ,in Europe, with only the narrow channel dividing them, English and French were fighting and killing one another, they were becoming united in this country for the sake of confederation. That is the proud part of our history, because the two races were united here long before the thunders of Trafalgar and Waterloo had died away. That is the spirit we need to-day, the spirit of conciliation, the spirit of compromise, and then the spirit of co-operation, if we wish to solidify and consolidate confederation. And in thinking how this might be brought about; it seems to me that if there is one man whose early history, whose long devotion to public duty in the service of humanity, whose whole life has led him to consider this question, I think he sits at times in this House-I do not know whether he is here or not now-his works as they have been laid before the world in the treatment of capital and labour, the two most difficult things in our social economy to unify, show that he did more to unite them than any other man in any country,-a man of whom it was said recently in Ottawa by a citizen of the neighbouring republic, "The greatest difficulties we have settled in the United States were settled on the basis of a charter provided for by your Prime Minister, W. L. Mackenzie King.1" And I say that spirit of conciliation has been the study of the Prime Minister's life. If that spirit is to be carried out, if these rifts, which some say exist in confederation, are to be closed, if there is any hope of keeping together the provinces and having them united in a happy and progressive country, I certainly believe that the Prime Minister is the man. who in the spirit he has displayed throughout his life is most likely'' to be effective in bringing about that great national undertaking.
Mr. .10ESN MORRISON (Weyburn):	Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of criticism of the government on this budget, and I realize it is much easier to be critical than to be correct, especially when one is serving the public. I am disappointed at the tardiness of the government in not making more tariff
The Budget-Mr. Morrison

reductions this year. Hon. members to my right are chronic fault-finders; of course, it is impossible for a government to please them. It seems to be the duty of an official opposition to find fault, whether things are right or not. They will always cry, "Wolf! Wolf!" when nothing is wrong, and the public have learned to recognize that, and consequently pay very little attention to their criticism. They have been tried and found wanting. They ask the people to hustle these inconsistent Liberals out of office and to put them in; but they have nothing new to offer, nothing constructive. They still talk about the alleged virtues and sing the praises of protection, and attribute to the protective system any prosperity that we have attained in Canada. I submit that we have succeeded so far in spite of the protection afforded to the manufacturers which has borne heavily upon the rest of the people. The customs tariff is to the manufacturers and Conservative politicians a cure-all patent medicine. They claim it will raise our revenues by the duties collected on incoming goods. Yet they want it mule-high, bull-strong and pig-tight so as to stop all goods coming in. They decry free trade as ruinous, but they would go to the other extreme and have "no trade or truck with the Yankees"-Canada's best customers. That was their cry in 1911 when agriculture in Canada and all allied industries received a body blow from which this country has not recovered to this day. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we suffered a greater monetary loss through the defeat of reciprocity in 1911 than we did from the Great war.
I think the government should have taken the duties off automobiles and auto trucks this session, removed the duties on cotton goods, and lowered the duties on many of the necessities of life. I should like to buy a new car this year. Would the Finance Minister advise me to buy a Canadian-made car or an imported car?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Buy an imported car
and turn the duty into the treasury.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I buy an imported
car the price I pay is the actual market value, plus duty, and I turn a few hundred dollars into the federal treasury. Would that not be a more patriotic thing to do than to buy a car from a Canadian multi-millionaire and turn the tax into his private coffer? I find the idea spreading considerably in the west that if we cannot get the tariff duties lowered in any other way we shall have to start a propaganda in favour of buying imported goods in preference to the home made,

thereby helping the Finance Minister to balance his budget.
The United States have put a tariff of 42 cents against Canadian wheat for home consumption, but they admit it free of duty when used in milling for export purposes. Our wheat is required to be blended with the United States wheat for home consumption. That makes it expensive for the American consumer, and it is also a hardship on the Canadian producer. A restriction of this character injures both parties. Would the matter be improved any by Canada putting an export duty on wheat, thereby curtailing the ability of the American millers to compete with Canadian flour in the world's market? Would it not be a much better plan for Canada to send an ambassador or a high commissioner to Washington, accompanied by a competent staff, in order to keep American public men properly informed as to Canadian conditions instead of trying to fight them? I believe that if we had had an ambassador or a good Canadian representative, at Washington the Fordney tariff would never have been imposed against us. If we had had such a representative at Washington the Chicago drainage canal would never have come into use, and our interests and the interests of shipping on the'Great Lakes, both Canadian and American, would have been protected. Figures have been submitted to the House showing that millions of dollars annually are lost through the lowering of the levels of the Great Lakes. A great deal of this loss is passed on to Canadian manufacturers and Canadian farmers; as a matter of fact we all have to share it. Had we had a representative at Washington to present our case properly this loss might have been averted. It is much better statesmanship to make provision in advance and prevent a possible injury from being done than it is to try and devise a cure after the event has happened. The United States has been our best customer and Great Britain second. Our trade with the United States last year was over $900,000,000. Yet some people say we should have no truck or trade with that country.
The budget, I think, should be clarified by the Acting Minister of Finance. The estimates of ordinary expenditure for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1925, amounted to $381,949,379.67. If we deduct the appropriations for railways, amounting to $56,000,000, it would leave $325,949,379.67. Now on page 32 of the Canadian National railway report we find that the amount of $8,491,553.57 was loaned to the system by the government. The

The Budget-Mr. Morrison
estimates for the last fiscal year as they passed the House amounted to $329,086,395.97. The Finance Minister estimated the expenditure for the same period on February 28, 1925, as $319,700,000, the amount saved or unexpended would be $9,386,305.97. The latter amount is an apparent saving on the year's expenditure, but the Acting Minister of Finance gives no explanation of the manner in which so large an amount has been saved or unexpended, and takes no credit for what is, if actually achieved, a remarkable performance. If this amount had not been saved or unexpended, instead of a surplus of $1,820,000 there would have been a deficit of $7,500,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me ask: How can Canada properly balance her budget? To this question I reply: By increasing production per capita; by increasing her population; by decreasing public expenditure; by getting nearer sound business methods for conducting the public business. I have obtained figures from the Bureau of Statistics as to yields of wheat in nine European countries and find that the average yield per acre for five years, from 1917 to 1921 inclusive, for the countries mentioned is as follows:
Bushels
per acru
Germany	 26.4
Austria	 15.4
Belgium	 35.6
Bulgaria	 13.4
Denmark	 43.9
France	 19.9
England and	Wales	 31.2
Norway	 24.6
Czechoslovakia	 20.8
This is an average of 25.8 bushels per acre. In those same years the average in Canada was 12.8, just half the yield per acre of these European countries. The average acreage in Canada in this period1 was 18,546,000 acres. At thirteen bushels extra per acre, this would mean 241,098,000 bushels. Other grains would double this total! of increased wealth. Acreage can and I think would be doubled1 if indbee-ments for profitable farming were held out in Canada. I would like our protectionist friends to consider what such production of wealth from agriculture would mean to industries generally. Suppose that they merely get their share of it, in the open competitive market, would it not be better for them to take a smaller margin ,of profit on a maximum output and keep their factories running to capacity? Would that pay our railroads to operate to maximum capacity? Would it not be better for our financial institutions and for all the people generally rather than that
restrictions should be put on the basic industries so that there is no inducement for people to work at these industries. The basic industries of the country have to be on a properly sound basis before real stable conditions can. be obtained for the dependent industries. It would be also better for labour. There would' be much work in the country. Our protectionist friends are very solicitous for the poor working man, especially coming near election time; but if we had: a maximum production and1 smaller profits, with a maximum turnover, there would1 be no idleness in the country. These poor yields of Canadian farms are not because the soil is poor or because Canadians are poor farmers, but there is a real cause for that How yield and I consider it is the excessive cost of farming ;n Canada. It is often impossible to farm profitably. Lumber and building materials generally, farm materials and farm supplies of all kinds are much too costly. It is a physical impossibility for men to carry the burden of somebody else and do their best in business. The same thing applies to industry. If an industry is burdened it cannot do its best. Every time tan unfair burden is imposed on a man you decrease his productive ability and the same thing applies to an industry.
At a meeting of the Brantford Board of Trade, held on March 14, 1911, the following resolution, proposed by Mr. Harry Cockshutt, at present Lieutenant Governor of Ontario, was adopted:
Resolved,-Our (1) material, (2) national and (3) empire interests will be best served by keeping entirely free of reciprocity entanglements with the United States at the present time. Carried 53 to 49.
About two years after this I was in Minneapolis and I saw the Cockshutt implements there selling in competition with American implements. I was in a wholesale implement warehouse., and I asked the manager how those implements compared in the amount of sales with the American implements and he said, "Oh they get their share of the trade" I was surprised to learn that the, prices of Cockshutt implements in Minneapolis were very much lower than they were in Winnipeg. Unfortunately I did not take down the figures and cannot quote them, but they were very much cheaper in Minneapolis than in Winnipeg. It shows that when the Canadian manufacturer wants to compete with the American he can do so. Some people think that the Canadian manufacturer pays the duty on his implements going across the line, that he is handicapped and prevented from getting into the American market. There is

The Budget-Mr. Morrison
no handicap whatever. But the American is handicapped by the tariff in getting into our market. The Canadian manufacturer has that one hundred and ten million American market on the same terms as he has the Canadian market. He has the drop on the American manufacturer to that extent. The Brantford people are really high protectionists. I do not know why they send a gentleman down here posing as a Liberal. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Raymond) was finding fault with the Conservatives for their indefiniteness in their statements about the tariff. I do not agree with my Conservative friends about their customs tariff, but I must say that they come out and say where they are at. They state what they believe with regard to the tariff and our Liberal friends are disappointing the country. They have a good policy. They have one policy to preach at election time, to get into power. They appeal to the public on a low tariff policy, and when they get here it would take a magnifying glass to find out the difference between a Liberal and a Conservative when it comes to the tariff. It cannot be done. It is all popycock. About three weeks ago Lieutenant Governor Coekshutt toured western Canada as an emissary for the high protectionists. He handed out a lot of fine stuff about a "get together spirit" between the east and west, just what the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) shot across the floor of the House a little while ago. He says "Let us get together, in a spirit of conciliation and good will"; but back in 1911 he did all in his power to take our natural markets from us. He has the same spirit yet, though he is a Conservative, exactly as the hon. member for Brantford is a good Liberal-no difference at all. I want to tell my hon. friend how we can have a good spirit of unity without going out west and waving the flag. That trip out west was only an admission that down in their hearts they realized that something is really wrong. The right way to overcome all this illfeeling which is growing, and this difference between east and west, between urban and rural, is just to give the common fellow a square deal, and there would be no need for flag-waving. The common people get no favours, and they should no longer be imposed upon. They are not satisfied to sit still and be imposed upon.
With reference to the tariff board which my hon. friend talks about, to advise the government as to what duties should be put on the different implements, I ask, has any manufacturer gone to any government, Liberal or Conservative, asking that duties be imposed on competitors, where the government have re-

plied, "All right, sir, put all your cards on the table and we will look into the matter?" Did hon. members ever hear of that? I .never saw it. It is time they got someone to inform them. I do not believe a tariff board in the hands of such gentlemen .would be anything more than something to hide behind. Certainly they will put on the board men who believe in a protective system, and they will get the report from these men and say, "Here is what is recommended' to us." They will make them the goat, and we will be the burden-bearers as usual.
A lot of this inability to compete with outsiders is due to difficulties of the home-made variety. For instance, not long ago I cut a clipping from a Montreal paper with reference to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company having watered stock. They watered the stock in that company four times the amount they actually put in, and then they charged rates to pay dividends of seven per cent all these years. Here is the dope that the Montreal manufacturers swallowed. Their employees were charged four times the rate for their light bill, and it made living in Montreal very expensive. Whenever a new company started to supply heat, power and light, the old ring would get after it and give a good inducement to it to come into the combine. This was done until they got a combine capitalized at something like 1164,000,000. This was over capitalization all tacked on to the cost of the product of the factory, because it makes living expenses higher and the companies accordingly have to pay higher wages. Then they keep their competitors out with a tariff wall and the}' say:	Charge it to the farmers of the
west; they are making money; they can pay it. A few years ago when a Toronto manufacturer was trying to shake me on this tariff question, I asked him: "Why do you not even sell us your goods for the same price plus extra freight charges, at which you sell them to the Ontario and Quebec farmers?" He said: "Look here, Morrison, you know the way business is done-all that the traffic will stand. You fellows are making more money and you can afford to pay more than the Ontario farmers can. We have got you farmers down where we want you and we are going to make you pay. If the position was reversed, you would do the same." After talking about two hours, he got impatient, finding that he could not get away with his guff, and so he spoke out the truth.
Employers who enjoy special privileges either by protection, or bonus, can give a better inducement to labour than the farmer can, but they do so only at the demand of the labour unions. Their bonus is the farmer's burden,

The Budget-Mr. Morrison
as we cannot compete in the labour market. The result is that Canada's output per acre of farm products is only one-half of what it would otherwise be.
Canada needs more workmen to work and develop her basic industries, and care should be exercised in getting immigrants. Better inducements will have to be given in order to keep people on the land. To start immigrants farming the first year they are in Canada is a Serious mistake, because such a practice results in their losing their money. Then, of course, the country is knocked, and efforts at immigration abroad are undone. A man should be in this country for at least one season and acquire some experience, before he invests his little bit of money. It should be an easy matter to compel every immigrant to have in his possession as a part of his passport, a document in his own language, furnished foy this government, setting out clearly Canadian conditions, and the Canadian immigration law. This would do away altogether with the old cry of deception which so many immigrants put up when they lose their harvest earnings in a poker game. People coming to us from the British Isles are particularly faulty in this regard. This could easily be set right if some one seriously minded was interested.
Experience on Canadian farms is necessary, for one year at least, and settlers should be established or domiciled within already improved municipal areas, which now have railroad, roads, schools, churches and post offices, It is folly to put them away back too far from these conveniences. Conditions would be too bad for them and many of them would become dissatisfied. It is unnecessary to provide more public utilities to take care of the increased population until those municipalities which have those conveniences and have to pay for them are better settled. Conditions have changed much for pioneers within the past twenty-five years.
We need an agricultural credits' system as is recommended by Dr. Tory in his report. On page 12 of Dr. Tory's report, he states:
I have discussed the problem with many business men in the east and in the west, men who know the difficulties associated with the building up of successful enterprises and I have not met one who would say that he believed that any business-farming or other,- which did not have the advantage of a protected market, or of patent rights, which in some measure gave a monopoly, could continue to prosper, paying 8 per cent or 10 per cent for capital, and a like amount for current borrowings. With this opinion my own judgment is in complete accord.
Capital and labour must learn to cooperate and fairly to recognize their inter-146
dependence. Western Canada needs more of both, working harmoniously. Wasteful competition of our two big railway systems must cease. We can no longer pay rates to maintain public-utility corporations overlapping and duplicating services. Our banks, retail coal companies, retail lumber-yard companies, newspaper publishing companies, and others, are all meeting the new conditions by getting together, one firm closing in one town, their rival closing in another town. They have been forced to co-operate or perish. Let our railways do likewise, and cut down their unnecessary overhead costs, instead of moving heaven and earth to get higher rates. This country cannot prosper under higher rates. I have been enumerating some of the industries that have closed some of their branch offices, and I would submit that some of these institutions are amongst the 2,000 that have closed their doors in the last few years. I believe there will be a few more that will close on the same basis, but business is improving with it all.
Those of us who have to pay freight charges, Largely both ways, are very much interested in getting better rates. We have to pay the freight on our purchases of implements, twine, lumber and coal, and again we have to pay the freight on our live stock and grain going out. We are intensely interested in seeing efficiency in railway management.
I am going to mention a matter that is not altogether federal, but something will have to be done to remedy the situation. Last fall a taxation conference was held at Ottawa and the Dominion and provincial governments sent representatives. The object of the conference was to define more clearly the respective spheres of taxation, and to eliminate all unnecessary duplication. I do not know what measure of success attended their efforts, or whether they accomplished anything to benefit the heavily taxed citizen. I am about to cite a case in dispute between the provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia and this case is typical of many others. A farmer from Saskatchewan moved to British Columbia where he died three years later. He had sold three farms on agreements of sale. The British Columbia government collected succession duties on those agreement-of-sale contracts, and to-day the Saskatchewan government is trying to collect succession duty on the sarnie agreements of sale. I am not accusing the Saskatchewan government nor excusing the British Columbia government. I know all the parties concerned, and I know it is very hard on the widow and

The Budget-Mr. Morrison

the children to have to pay -the succession duty twice. Succession duties on bequests outside of a province come doubly high at any time, but to have to pay them twice is very unfair. The federal government should call another taxation conference as soon as possible at which all the provinces should be represented. As regards any matters on which they cannot agree, let them decide at this conference that they will split the difference fifty-fifty until they get -from the Privy Council a decision on the matter. I spoke to our Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) who, I know, is not responsible in any measure. Hie told me that he could no nothing and he advised me that they could take the matter to the Privy Council. What a privilege! The widowed mother would have a fat chance to take her case to the Privy Council. She would have no chan-ce at all. She will have to pay the duty twice if those men will not compromise and go fifty-fifty on this tax. I do not think that the governments of these provinces should be allowed to demand the tax a second time; that is getting down pretty near to what we might call tyranny.
On page 4690 of Hansard, volume V, 1924, the following question by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), together with the reply by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), is reported:
On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. W. C. Good (Brant): Would the Prime Minister give the House an assurance that the Alternative Vote bill, which had already received its first reading, will receive consideration early next session, and further that there will be no election, as far as he can guarantee that, between now and then?
Mr. Mackenzie King: In reply to the first question, I may say that if we are all here when parliament re-assembles, certainly this alternative vote measure will be one of the first to be brought before the House.
I wish the Prime Minister were in his seat to tell us why this matter has not been brought before the House. It is very necessary if he intends to bring it down that he should move quickly, if he does not want to put all the blame, in the event of its being deferred, upon the poor old Senate. The Senate has its own burdens to bear. I think the Prime Minister should have lived up to his promise and brought down this legislation.
On page 1475 of Hansard of the present year the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in introducing his budget gave notice of the following resolution with regard to the Special War Revenue Act.
Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend The Special War Revenue Act, 1915, and to provide:-
1. That "cheque" shall be further defined to include any document or writing, not drawn upon or addressed to a bank, in exchange for which a bank

makes payment of a sum of money, except a coupon and a document used solely for the purpose of settling or clearing any account between banks, and that such a cheque shall be liable to the stamp tax imposed on cheques by the said act.
That I contend is singling out a certain class of people in the country for another extra burden-I refer especially to the creameries. We farmers know that when a man sends his can to the creamery he gets a receipt or ticket, and according to this proposed legislation he will be taxed on a dollar or two dollars receipt. We would not object if everybody were treated alike and if this provision read, " 'Cheque' shall be further defined to include any document for $10 or over." We do object, however, to being singled out for a tax like this, especially in view of the fact that the Acting Minister of Finance took care to retain the good will of those gentlemen who are fortunate enough to have the pleasure of clipping coupons, which are exempt from taxation. That is rubbing it in with a vengeance, and the government cannot expect Progressives, who are largely representatives of farmers, to stand for additional burdens. It is not a square deal; all should be treated alike. Why exempt the rich man and- tax the farmer engaged in the dairy business?

Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I had practically finished speaking. There is one other matter to which I wish to refer, and that is the case of the Home Bank depositors. When the Prime Minister toured western Canada last fall he was interviewed by committees of the Home Bank depositors for a statement as to what the government intended to do for them. He promised them that the government would bring down a bill this session for the relief of the Home Bank depositors, but he warned them that the Senate had the last say, as they did in the case of the branch lines bill of the 1924 session. Since the Prime Minister and the government realize this, I would urge upon them the necessity for immediate action in bringing down- a bill for the relief of these depositors. The distress that has followed the failure of the Home Bank is widespread, and the government will certainly share the blame if the measure of relief that is proposed is not brought down in plenty of time to enable the Senate to deal with it.

The Budget-Mr. Dechene

Mr. Speaker, the discussion on the budget resolution and its amendment by the hon. members who preceded me in this debate, only tend to show, first, that no one gives a thought to the Tory amendment, and secondly that, for the greater part, the attitude taken by the government in the present circumstances is justifiable and is the only reasonable one.
In fact, the Tory amendment has been entirely lost sight of. Very few of the hon. Conservative members themselves have ever taken the trouble of discussing it. The public has a right to wonder if this amendment were moved in good faith to expound a programme and the policy of a party, or if it were not simply a means of obstruction, by which they tried to prevent the Progressive party from introducing an amendment themselves, which might have had for effect-although one may question the fact-to throw into the discussion new ideas which might lead to a policy productive of results and aiming to create useful developments in our trade and administration. The Tory amendment had as a result the setting aside of the one moved by the Progressive party and to prevent, to some extent, any move which might bring on a discussion capable of producing effective measures for the welfare of the country. It is not astonishing therefore, that the Conservative amendment was entirely ignored, and that even the press of the country paid no attention to it; the amendment was given a public funeral, as it well deserved.

speechtext:
More than once, in the course of this debate, we have heard certain members demand new markets for our products. It is the proper time to examine what the present government has done to obtain more favourable openings for Canadian products. If we review the legislation already enacted, if we look into the treaties negotiated under the present regime, we may designate this government as: the government of trade conventions.
We notice in that sphere considerable activity. Indeed, never have there been as many trade conventions directly negotiated between Canada and other countries, as by the present government. These various conventions have brought us important business. That is a worthy achievement for which we must give thanks especially to the hon. gentlemen who negotiated the treaties. As a result, have we not noticed that our exports have increased in a most extraordinary way? If we consider one kind of products only, we are aware, for instance, that our exports of farm products amount to more than $500,000,000 which is equivalent- to more than half our total export trade of $1,070,611,616.
In fact, in 1922, we exported farm products to the amount of $532,820,457.
In 1923-a year after the present government came to power-our exports of said products amounted to $553,069,240, that is already an increase of $21,000,000.
In 1924, we continued our ascending march; our exports amounted to $598,729,385, in farm products alone, that is more than half of the total exports of this country. The result of this large exportation of our farm products has been of a twofold nature: first it brought considerable revenue to the country and, secondly it has stabilized prices in this country. Indeed, if our exports had not been greater than what they were during the last years of the Conservative government, I think that the price of farm products in this country would have been so low that most of the farmers would have been forced to abandon their farms; however, under the present administration, thanks to the trade conventions signed with various countries, we have noticed a great improvement. The

The Budget-Mr. Dechene
farmers throughout the country must be pleased with the results obtained in so short a time.
One of the tariff measures most criticized was the preference which Canada gives to the products imported from Great Britain. Often, when something goes wrong in a city, we hear: Oh! this is caused by the British preference. In the course of the budget discussion, which has been going on for nearly a month, very few speakers seem to have gone to the trouble of informing us as to what the British preference has cost us and what are its benefits. The British preference applies not only to Great Britain and Ireland, but it applies also to all the various colonies or dominions which make up the empire, when these dominions grant us a preferential tariff of a likewise nature. Our best client for farm products is, without any doubt, England herself. In fact, out of the $598,729,385 of agricultural products exported during the year 1924, our exports to England amounted to $337,813,146; this means that more than half of our exports to England consists of the products or by-products of the farm. This seems to be quite an excellent reason in favour of the preferential system; however, there is also the reverse side of the medal to look at:	What do we import? That is
especially what is considered ruinous for our country. If we stop a moment to consider the total products imported from England, we notice what others have observed before us, what Benjamin B. Wallace, of the United States Tariff Commission, has himself stated in the annals of the American Academy of the political and Social Sciences. This gentleman, who devotes his time to economic questions, tells us-I may state broadly-that the British preference granted in 1896 did not prevent the decrease of Great Britain's share of trade in the products which she exported to Canada. This is not a Canadian, or an Englishman, but an American who is struck by the fact that this preference did not prevent Great Britain losing ground and witnessing the decrease of her percentage in products exported to Canada. And he gives the following list: in 1883, our imports from Great Britain amounted to 42.3 per cent of the total imports; in 1893, the decrease had already begun to be felt and these imports amounted to only 35.5 per cent; in 1903, the downward trend continued, these imports amounting only to 25.2 per cent of the total imports; in 1914, we notice the same downward trend 21.3 per cent; in 1923, the English share of trade had still decreased and the British imports amounted to only 17.6 per cent of our total
imports; in 1924, after the tariff changes so much criticized, we still notice that the figures have again fallen, and that the imports which come from England amount to only 17.02 per cent of our total imports. According to the statistics of this American gentleman, I think that the British preference has not been so unfavourable to us as one wants us to believe.
However^ our imports from the United States have followed an absolutely different course, they have always been on the increase and the percentage of American goods corn-spared with that of goods imported from other countries indicates a continuous increase, and this notwithstanding that there exists no preferential tariff in favour of the United States. We quite often hear-we have heard it in the House on a number of occasions-members quote instances of industries being ruined by this British preference.
I shall myself give, as briefly as possible, examples of the conditions of some of these industries, and I think that the instances I shall quote to the House will suffice to prove that one tries to throw the blame on the Imperial preference for all the evils which we suffer, from wherever they may come from.
For instance, one often hears of the boot and shoe industry. The statistics in regard to this industry afford us a very striking example. For an industry "ruined", it seems to enjoy a most marked activity. From 1921 to 1923 inclusively, the number of boot and shoe factories in Canada has increased from 177 to 186. The value of the output of these [DOT] factories increased from $44,665,381, in 1921, to $45,596,012, in 1923. The 1924 figures have not yet been compiled.
There is, therefore, an increase of nearly a million dollars in the output of boots and shoes in this country for the said period. The absurdity of the assertion that this industry is ruined owing to an unfair competition by the manufacturers of Great Britain, due to the preferential tariff is clearly seen by comparing the imports of boots and shoes from Great Britain and the domestic output. Although the imports of Great Britain have increased somewhat owing to a higher preference, the total is not sufficient to seriously hurt the Canadian manufacturers. With a domestic output amounting to $45,596,012, in 1923, the British imports were only $604,472.
The increase in 1924 only brought up this figure to a little more than one million dollars, to be exact $1,018,082, or again one forty-fifth of the Canadian production.
The Budget-Mr. Dechene

On the other hand to counteract this increase, we have a decrease in the imports of boots and shoes coming from the United
States. The decrease, in 1924, amounted to $121,465 compared with the imports of 1923. The net increase of foreign competition, amounts to $292,091, this is therefore far inferior to one per cent of the total domestic expenditure and gives a smaller percentage in increase than the home production. I therefore, think that these figures are sufficient proof to us that it is not the British preference which causes trouble to the manufacturers of this country. They can hold their own against foreign competition in other countries where' they sell their goods; I therefore see no reason why they cannot face British competition in our own country.
Another industry that we often hear about and which is occasionally pointed to as ruined, is the woollen industry.
In 1924, Canada purchased nearly $2,000,000 less of wool and woollen goods, than in 1923. As it is stated that British preference has the effect of ruining the Canadian woollen industry, it is interesting to note that in regard to the wool bought from the United Kingdom, there has been a decrease of nearly $2,500,000 in 1924, compared with 1923. The figures are as follows: in 1923, the imports of wool from England amounted to $35,520,730; in 1924, the figures are $33,163,186. During the same period there has also been a decrease of $556,778 in the purchase of woollen goods coming from the United States.
The woollen industry in Canada has not been . the only one to suffer in the world crisis of woollen and cotton goods. I shall call as a witness Mr. Pierce, President of the American Woollen Company. The latter in submitting the yearly report of said company, stated that the depression in the trade of American woollen goods, in 1924, had been the worst since the year of the Civil war. The loss of $11,970,000 sustained last year, by that company is the greatest deficit which it has ever had to register.
I think that the statement of Mr. Pierce clearly indicates that the woollen industry was still in a worse state in the United States than it was in Canada, and that it is not the British preference, nor even the general tariff which is the 'cause of the depression Which we may have had to suffer from in this country, however, if there was quite a marked depression, in 1921-22, in 1922-23, we notice already an improvement. In fact, there were, in 1922, 137 woollen mills, at present there are 141; the capital invested in this industry

increased from $37,102,382, in 1922, to $43,148218, in 1923, that is an increase of over $6,000,000. The output which amounted to 29,062,751 pounds, in 1922, had increased to 33,472,087 pounds, in 1923, that is an increase of 11,000,000 pounds. For an industry which is being ruined, really I think it is very fortunate. There are many people who would like to be ruined in that way.
The cotton industry also suffered considerably, and the opponents of British preference delighted in spreading that it was due to that "bugaboo" and that English and American cotton goods were ruining us, especially the English cotton goods.
During the year 1923, the imports to Canada of cotton goods decreased nearly $4,000,-000-$3,849,689 to be exact. The imports from the United Kingdom, under the British preference amounted to $538,100 less than in 1923. This is only another proof that conditions are improving in our home industry, and that there is an increase in the purchase of raw cotton for our Canadian mills. For the following three years the imports are these: In 1922, $22,455,546; in 1923, $30,780,915, and in 1924, $25,576,764.
In a word, the cotton industry has always been improving in this country, and I do not think that there is cause to consider as serious the cry of alarm spread by the manufacturers who always seek more protection, without considering the true facts. The exact cause of the closing of cotton mills in this country, has not been the lack of markets, but is due to the bad cotton crops in the United States and to the high prices reached by the raw cotton in the countries where it is grown. These gentlemen seem to have reaped handsome profits. Their mills resumed work early in 1924; and I do not think they can claim that, if the 'business was not what they expected it to be, it is again due to the British preference. One of the general results of the British preference has been to serve as a lever or to stabilize prices in this country. Not only should the interests of manufacturers be considered, but also those of the consumer, of the masses.

speechtext:
Hear,
hear! It is the first word spoken on behalf of the consumer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) saying that it is the first word spoken on behalf of the consumers in the course of this debate. I thank him very much for the compliment, I fear, however, that is not quite exact, because, in the course of his splendid speech, he has given us proof that, he, him-

The Budget-Mr. Dechene
self, takes an interest also in the consumer, and with success.
It is flattering to be able to point out to tourists, in a city, twenty, thirty, forty or fifty homes of millionaires and add:	These
are the owners of the large mills of this country, the masters of the working classes, that live there, they are responsible for the good and bad times; we must not forget, on the other hand, that apart from the millionaire, there is the people, the consumer. The millionaire does not make the wealth of a country. It is not because there are in the United States 125 millionaires possessing to themselves, one-tenth of the total wealth of the country, that the American Republic is wealthy! No, it is because the wealth is distributed among the masses. The manufacturer has no vested right to exact a living from the consumer; the industry is established to supply the consumer, generally, what he needs. It is the consumer who is the mainspring of all prosperity, of all national wealth in a country. It is, therefore important that the government should endeavour, as much as possible, to supply the consumer, the middle class of a country, the means of living comfortably, even with a certain ease, without for all that ruining the manufacturer. What makes the manufacturer prosperous, Sir, is the wealth of his client; the client of the manufacturer, is the consumer. You find the proof of this truth in the daily incidents of our Canadian national life. If in the west, the crops are bad, if prices are down, the client the consumer in the west is not rich, he buys little and he becomes a poor client for the manufacturer; however, let a good crop turn up, let the time come, when the financial conditions of that part of the country improve, immediately our fellow citizens of the west become buyers, become good clients and the manufacturer immediately benefits thereby. I think that the government is wise to give the greatest encouragement possible to the development of trade, especially to that of the farm products, so that the town people may get these products with the greatest facility possible, while allowing to the country people, the farmers, a fair profit which will permit them to better their lot and become good clients for the manufacturers.
I see, Sir, that I am enlarging somewhat on the subject. I shall try and be as brief as possible. I stated, at the outset of my remarks, that among our population, there existed too great a tendency, in certain parts of the country, at least, to expect everything from the government, and not to rely sufficiently on one's personal initiative or one's
judiciously concentrated effort to obtain excellent results, and I shall give a more striking instance of what can be done by the concentrated effort of a few to obtain a beneficial result for the masses. You will recall, Sir, that from the very first days of March, a group of members were striving to improve the lot of the rural classes, which constitute the greater part of their electors. The members who thus united were those of lower Quebec. They chose a chairman and, under the direction of the latter they immediately settled down to the task of obtaining results which they thought would be beneficial to their electors. Briefly, this was the problem: The southern part of Quebec has to put up with the same isolation as that of the northeastern part of New Brunswick. These gentlemen met so as to consider if it was possible to improve the conditions of their people and to better the means of shipping the potato crop which they produce in large quantities in that region. The market seemed closed to them. They live in the most remote eastern parts of the country. There existed a large market in the west which they had to reach at all cost, and this is the letter which these members sent to the chairman of the railway commission.
Ottawa, March 4 1925.
Dear Sin,-As Chairman of the deputation that visited you this morning, I beg to express our feeling of extreme gratitude for the kindly hearing and courtesy you have shown to our delegation to-day.
This deputation was composed of the following members of parliament:	Messrs. Pius Michaud
(Restigouche-Madawaska); J. G. Robichaud (Gloucester); W.. B. Snowball (Northumberland, N.B.); Aim6 Dechene (Montmagny); J. F. Fafard (L'Islet); F. J. Pelletier (Matane); George Bouchard (Kamou-raska); J. F. Pouliot (Temiscouta); Sir Eugent Fiset (Rianouski).
The main object of our deputation was to expose to your Lordship the awkward and extraordinary situation in which we, the representatives of the lower part of the province of Quebec and the upper parts of New Brunswick, are placed. Geographically speaking, we are situated at the tail-end of the western market and at the head of the eastern market. Apparently, we are like orphans, who do not belong to the respective provinces in which our counties are situated, and that is the main reason why we decided to approach your commission directly on behalf of our own population.
The main points that we discussed with your Lordship were: freight rates on potatoes, freight rates on lumber and express rates on fish; but the most pressing part of our problems at the present time are the freight rates on potatoes. Our population faces not only ruin and disaster, but on account of the extraordinary crop that was grown this year in the counties above mentioned (between 15,000,000 to 19,000,000 bushels of potatoes) the farmers, on account of the exorbitant rates that are being charged by the Canadian National Railway for the transportation of this product, which is the basis of the economic life of our population, are
The Budget-Mr. Dechene

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the year 1891 I appeared as a candidate for this House of Commons to represent the then old-time constituency of East York. I ran there as one who believed in the National Policy, as a disciple of Sir John A. Macdonald, and I have supported that policy all my life. I ran in that constituency as a
rather young man against a very important opponent, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, who had recently been Prime Minister. He had lost his seat in western Ontario. He carried East York and defeated me by a majority of 26. Within a year he died, and in 1892 I was elected to this House as the representative of that constituency. Ever since I have been in this House, and I have carried on pretty well the views I then held in regard to what I considered to be the proper tariff policy for this country. I came by my belief in the National Policy through my father, who was the first man in this country to organize the Manufacturers' Association, to develop what he called our "home industries," following somewhat the policy that had been adopted in the United States. It took a long while to build up industry there. They thought they were a sugar, cotton and corn growing country, but after a while the United States became the greatest manufacturing country in the world, largely because they adopted the policy of encouraging home industries. But in Canada it was rather hard work to get them going, and men like Isaac Buchanan-we do not hear much about him now-a Scotchman who had an idea that protection would be a good thing for this country, George Stephen, who afterwards became one of the founders of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and others who believed absolutely in the encouragement of home industries preached their faith. I might say that George Stephen was one of the first members of the Manufacturers' Association. I happen to know where a little book is that contains the names of those early members. Then John A. came along and took up the National Policy proposition, perhaps as a political manoeuvre-I will not say; I do not think so-but he was a strong believer so far as I ever knew in trying to do for Canada what the United States had already accomplished, to build up home industries and so give work to the people in manufacturing as well as in farming.
When I first came into this House in 1892 my constituency of East York had not a population of 25,000 people. It was made up of what is now called Greater Toronto, a rim of suburbs peopled by market gardeners, butchers, hog raisers and dairymen-a very ordinary lot of people. What has happened since? That once despised constituency of less than 25,000 people will be represented in the next House by eight members, who will speak for over 400,000 people To prove what I say I am going to name the constituencies that have come out of that hive Of all the mother constituencies in this country East York is
2292	COMMON'S
The Budget-Mr. Maclean (York)
the greatest. Out of that constituency the new House will have a member from South York with a population of 50,000. To-day I represent 120,000 people in this House, that being the population of only a portion of my original constituency. Next to South York there will be Toronto-Scarborough, another riding of over 60,000; then East Toronto, which I represented when it was called St. Matthew's ward-over the Don with only a few people living there but to-day it has a population of 60,000; then comes Northeast Toronto, which I represent to-day and where I hope my friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) will go, but they say he is looking in some other direction; that, too, is a great constituency. Then comes Northwest Toronto, which I represented for many years when it was in my original riding and was known as Toronto Junction, but which now comprises a great part of the city of Toronto;^ then I go over to Toronto-High Park, which I at one time represented in this parliament, another large constituencjr; then I come to that portion of West York which I represent to-day. ^ Under the adjustment that was made some time ago I am turning over probably some seventy polling subdivisions there that I represent in this House to-day. And lastly, and as the eighth of the lot, the township of Markham and her sister township, Vaughan, in West York go to North York taking with them the seed of the National Policy. That is eight constituencies that swarmed off from the original riding of East York that I represented. And I imagine that the feeling among that 400,006 people will be largely to maintain the policy which created the industries which support them, and which created and developed the great industries in many other parts of this country. Now you may call that part of the district suburban, it was only common township territory originally. What has happened to make this great change which resulted in one constituency growing into eight? It was the creation of a great many industries in Toronto and the establishment of those
400,000	people who believe in the National Policy. They believe in it for the reason- although my hon. friends the Progressives may object to it-that it builds up home industries. The Progressives say, and they are in favour of something in contra-distinction to the National Policy, that they do not want that in the west. Now I say and I challenge hon. members from the west to dispute it, that this is the view of the people in that part of Canada, namely-that the people of Winnipeg want their city to become a Toronto,

and the people of Edmonton also want their city to become a Toronto; and even the Progressives themselves, who profess a policy different from the National Policy adopted, do not believe in raising their families to become mere farmers. There is no farmer in the ranks of the Progressives that does not hope to see his sons have the opportunity to get into business, to get into industries, to get into mining, and all these other occupations. What they want in the west, and this is what I wish to tell my hon. friends-[DOT]
