speechtext:
I should like to correct
the hon. gentleman on that point.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend will have lots of opportunity to correct me. I will stand any amount of correction and I hope he will carry out his intention. I am sure he must want to see diversity of employment in this country. I have not seen a farmer from the west who does not want to see the same thing. You may ask "How is Toronto interested in that?" Well, I will tell you. This great community, now to be represented in the coming parliament by eight members, has a population, with enormous industries built up in that old East York, who believe in the National Policy, and who believe in diversity of employment. And the thing that makes a country .is diversity of employment, and that is what the issue in this coming election is to be. It is to be whether we are to have diversity of employment, or whether we are to have the development merely of one or two industries in this country and, in the main, agriculture.
I want to say something more about the people who make up that population of 400,000 to which I have referred. The bulk of them live in the East York that I have described. There are thousands and thousands of men and women who live there-not in the city of Toronto but still in old East York [DOT]-men and women who are on the payroll of industries located in the city of Toronto. These people have grown up and have raised their families there and they want to see this industrial growth and development kept up. They do not want to lose their houses; they want to see employment continued, and I may say that unemployment is the problem before this House and the country to-day. We have got to deal with it; it is a problem which exists all over the world to-day. It prevails in England. So bad is that problem in England that Mr. Baldwin, and some other prominent men there, are preaching something in the direction of the state financing work and helping to provide wages for the

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (York)
unemployed. Do not let my Progressive friends down the line run away with the idea that unemployment exists only in protectionist countries. Unemployment is worse in England than in many countries where they do not have free trade; and I may say that it. was free trade that first gave England diversity of employment. Perhaps, that raises an objection to my argument; but nevertheless the fact is that any country that wants to hold its own in the world to-day must not depend on one source of employment. There must be diversity of employment, there must be opportunity for every family. Every country now is up against this struggle for existence that is prevalent, and if there is to be diversity of employment it must be based on a policy of its own. In times of stress, and after the great war through which we have passed, the impelling principle is to keep your own work for your own people; keep your own markets for your own products and do not surrender them to other people. Germany is ready to raid our markets. She raided and fought us in war, and, now she is going to raid our industries. France feels the same way. The United States have got ahead, and I think would like to have possession of our markets.
On that line I want to tell the House another thing that happened. I went to a meeting last Saturday where they organized the new riding of South York and these questions came up. The most popular sentiment expressed there that day-and the audience consisted of the men and women who will make up the new South York, and who are living in that great community of 400,000 people-the sentiment that was expressed there, the sentiment that was applauded and was the predominant sentiment, was in regard to reciprocity of tariffs as between Canada and the United States. If they propose to bar us out and to take our markets, and if Germany purposes to invade our markets with a great cut in her prices, then we have to give treatment for treatment or we will be wiped out. There is a great new struggle going on now in the world between countries just to hold their own. It is a fight for existence; and the thought that is growing more and more among our people-it is growing in the minds of the
400,000	people who make up greater Toronto; the idea that impels them and comes home to every family; to the father who is employed, to the son and daughter who may be employed in these various industries or in other businesses-is how are we to keep our wages? More and more this demand is being made on the part of labour. You hear it all over
our country, you hear it in Montreal, you hear it in other parts of Canada, you even here it in the west. What we must do in this House, if we are to maintain the position of our country-I do not say that we have to go into an absurd system of protection-is to keep the work for our own people, and we will have to fight to do it. Our friends from the west want rather to reduce the little protection we have, and we have some protection. The issue I have described will be the fight in this coming election whenever it does come.
The members from the west will have to fight that very same question in their country. The people in the west have no intention of remaining a purely agricultural community. Towns there want to grow. You are building UP universities there. The farmers are sending their sons to the universities, and they will want the universities to be followed by scientific schools and to send their sons fo those schools; they will rvant to see the possibility of their having different employments. You cannot raise sons and make them all farmers. ^ That is the mistaken belief which my hon. friends down the line hold. You must have diversity of employment in order to provide occupation for all c.f your family Mv hon. friends to my left may find fault with the position I take, but I have been rather sympathetic with a great many of the things they advocate. I am entirely sympathetic with them in regard to their request for better ocean rates. I am sympathetic with what I have heard to-day in reference to reduced railway rates in this country, and the way to reduce those railway rates is to have an economic management of our railways and stop the awful competition. I am going to refer to that matter a little later on. We should also develop our waterways.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In regard to the establishment of industries in the west, does my hon. liend think we will be able to establish in-dustnes in the west without some protection from the competition of these large factories in Toronto?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a fair
question and I answer that I think so. I read in the Free Press of Winnipeg the other daj% the statement that new industries were coming in and the people out there were glad to welcome them. The farmers are developing new industries. They have gone into the business of (butter and dairying, and have made great advances in the live stock industry. They will have abattoirs and everything in that line. They are going to vary their occupations and their industries and build up
2294	COMMON'S
The Budget-Mr. Maclean (York)
their country, as Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime provinces have built up their country. In other words, you are going to see a revival of the idea that in order to build up a country you must have diversity of occupation and give encouragement to your own industries. If you like to give your industries away to other countries, you may do so, and your people will go away. However, 1 do not think that is the sentiment of the west. It is not the sentiment of British Columbia, or of the Maritime provinces. It is certainly not the sentiment of Quebec that they desire to see their industries go. Yet you would almost think that Quebec was ready to let her industries go. But that is not the popular view, and I am quite sure the province of Quebec will be heard from on this question before the next election is over.
I will tell the House now about the industries in my own comparatively small riding. Hon. members will ask, what are they made up of? Market gardeners started there years ago. There is a big market gardening industry in that district. I have lived among these market gardeners; they are constituents of mine. The industry does not look to be very much, but it gives homes to hundreds of them in that county. The next interest there is probably the berry and fruit industry. The fruit industry has developed largely. Next is the florist industry, developed by men who have greenhouses, glass houses and who do a great trade in flowers. The business has attained large proportions. It is a source of income and thousands of them are being supported by it. Hon. members talk about the export of poultry from the west. They ought to see the poultry and eggs that are raised in that small community now called South York, formerly called East York. It is an immense industry. They have also other associated interests of that kind, and all these people have an absolutely vital interest in remaining as they are in that district and having a chance to make their living, and they will only be able t,o make a living now if these home markets which they have at present are kept for them. I pointed out to the hon. leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) the other day that one difficulty these men in South York labour under is the seasonal advantage our competitors in the United States have, because their season over there is much earlier than ours and there are large importations from the States which are bought by the rich people of Toronto. Other towns of Ontario are in the same position. But that market is liable to be raided, and is raided as a matter of fact, by the competi-
tion of the United States. I think those people are entitled to some kind of protection. They are asking for it and I am putting in a plea that those industries ought to be protected and kept there. They have a right to have their interests advocated in this House.
The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) this afternoon said a great deal about compromise and co-operation. Well, there must be some kind of co-operation between the east and the west, and some day it will come. Some day the most pronounced protectionist in this country will come from the west and he will be in favour of great big interests and local interests being built up by some kind of national policy for protection, to keep a lot of work for our own people and a lot of our own products for our own market. What would I suggest? I am not speaking for one moment for the manufacturing interests. The manufacturers themselves have not many great friends in this country now. They are doing most of the talking themselves. They think of nothing but themselves, and some of them are very selfish. A great many of them 'made enormous profits in the recent war. Now they are enjoying games of golf and riding in great big cars, and people are making a clamour about them. I am saying nothing about this. Let them look out for themselves, but I speak for those on the pay-rolls of the industries of this country.
We have heard something about export duties, and we have those duties in this country. The government has placed an export duty on power. I listened this afternoon to the hon. member for London (Mr. White) who opposed it, or rather said it should not be brought into force until the present contracts ran out. That may or may not be true, but Canada to-day has enormous water powers, especially in the region of Hudson bay, and north of the western provinces. I believe all those water powers can be harnessed, and by means of long distance and high transmission, perhaps by wireless transmission, there will be great abundance of power development in that country which may be a great source of revenue to Canada and to all the provinces. There are other things we can accomplish by an export duty. Do you believe I would let one pound of nickel go out of this country to go to Mond's smelters in England or to the International Nickel Company in the United States? There is not a pound of nickel ore in any place but Canada, and I would not let a pound go out without being absolutely refined in Canada;

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (York)
and yet through Sir Alfred Mond and the International Nickel Company-and they are the only people who got the ore-Germany got all the nickel she wanted during the war, and she got it from the nickel ore in Canada.
I have made that statement before, and have been condemned for it, but I say it again, and I appeal to the people of Canada through their representatives at Ottawa, to place a duty on the export, not only of power, if they are in favour of it, but on nickel, in order that it may be refined and made into metal in this country.
I would also put an - export duty on pulp-wood going out of Canada, which would help our revenues. The settler will say, "I have only one market for my pulpwood and it is the export market." That may be true, but let his own province establish a pulp mill to grind his pulp, and in that way we will have the business in our own country. We command the bulk of the pulpwood business of the world, and we can get the whole of the business, on account of the class of pulpwood we have in Canada. We have to take care of that pulpwood and I think we will take care of it. As long as we have it we can get a great revenue from it, and an export duty placed on pulpwood will help pay the taxes and debts of the country.
I am going to leave the tariff question with this brief statement of my views. I happen to come from that little constituency which has grown from 25,000 people to 400,000 people and that has the greatest collection of industries of any portion of Canada. That constituency is growing; the people are growing with it, and they have as much right to claim fair treatment as the people of any other portion of this country. When these conflicting claims arise, there is only one way, as was said by the hon. member for Brantford this afternoon, by which they can be settled. There must be some compromise, some adjustment, made and some patriotic view taken that we want to help our own people and our own industries in a time of trial such as this.
I am going to pass from that to discuss for just a moment the banking conditions of this country. I am an absolute believer in Canada adopting, as far as it can be adapted to this country, the national reserve bank system of the United States. I have already said in this House that the greatest public ownership proposition in the world today is the national reserve bank system of the United States. It is absolutely owned by the people of the United States and billions of gold owned by the people of that country
are behind it. They have also their own coinage systems, and the whole credit of the United States is behind the national reserve bank system. The way in which the United States is now and has been able for some years to encourage the farming industry and to expand it, is by providing a credit system for the farmers with absolute security and guarantee. That is done through this national reserve bank system. That system has been an immense success in the United States, and we in this country, and especially the people in the west, want a similar banking system. The Canadian banks, however, are opposed to this, for what reason I do not know. They should not have any objection to doing what has been so successful in the United States. The United States is going to do the reparation work of the world in the way of financing; she is doing it now for France and Germany; she has helped England immensely; she is ready to do this for all the world, through the fact that she has this splendid system of banking backed by the whole credit of that country. Our banks oppose the establishment of a similar institution in Canada and they say: Oh, we might get the system of banking they have in the United States and some money might be lost. Let me tell the banks of this country what I would like to see because of the failure of our banks to take advantage of the creation of a national reserve bank system in Canada. I would like to see fifty bankers from the little towns and villages throughout the whole of the United States come to Canada and ask for charters for small national banks to develop here. If our bankers saw such an influx into this country of the same system of banking as they have in 'the United States, backed by the national credit, there would be a wonderful improvement in our financing. Branch bank business, as far as we know it, is not a success. It is ending more and more in mergers. I wish the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) were here to-night so that I could tell him what is going on. Within five or six years, at the rate at which mergers are taking place, we shall have not more than five or six banks in this country. Let me enlighten the House and the country about three very surprising morgues that are maintained in Canada. A morgue is a place where dead things are kept. What do hon. members think these three great, big morgues contain? One, I think, is in Toronto and perhaps two are in Montreal. They are the storehouses of the banks' safes that have been discarded be-
2296	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Maclean (York)
cause of the bank mergers that have taken place in Canada. Hundreds of agencies were closed, for instance, the Merchants Bank and the Molson's Bank, and in Montreal there were others besides these. There have been numerous mergers in Ontario. Now, owing to these bank mergers, there are nearly
20,000	of these safes stored in this country, and the banks do not know what to do with them. They are afraid to show them and they keep them hidden. That is a result of the bank mergers. But the bank mergers have not finished, and I am going to make this prediction that as soon as this parliament is over, there will be three great mergers in Toronto. They are all arranged now so far as I can gather, and they will go on. Let there be big banks if there must; but let there be little banks as well, and let the little banks have the same advantage of the national credit as they have in the United States and as the big banks have in this country. The big banks may say that I am making an attack on them. I am not. I want the big banks to make more money than they are making now. All I am asking is that they will give more service. If we have something like that in this country, many things will take place that will help to bring about a recovery m business conditions.
I should like to refer for a moment to the question of the revision of our constitution and of making our courts supreme. I heard an lion, member from the west speak this afternoon about a grievance that existed there in regard to tax duties on agreements of sale whereby an innocent family, that owned property in one province and that had gone to live in another, found that both provinces claimed the tax and they had to pay the tax in the two places. The provinces said to them:	You pay the tax
in the meantime and go to the Privy Council in England to have the matter settled. We shall never be a country until we interpret our own laws in our own country iby our own courts. That is a question on which all the Canadian people can unite. The greatest court in the world to-day is the Supreme Court of the United States and it was built up by American lawyers. They have become great jurists and they have a splendid system of law in that country. The crowning glory of the United States is probably its own Supreme court and the integrity of that court and many other courts over there. Canada will never be able to hold up her head alongside of the United States until she has at least as good a banking system and as good a final 
court system as they have there, instead of being, as we are, minors, wards, and having to go to the Old Country in order to have our laws interpreted. The people in the Old Country are quite willing that we should interpret our own laws and to allow us to make our own constitution. Speaking of these constitutional questions, I say that much headway was made in this parliament this session when the motion of an hon. member from the west in favour of Senate reform was accepted, went through and was recognized in Great Britain. Results will come from it in a very short time, and you will see Canada having a much better position amongst the nations of the world than she has to-day.

speechtext:
Are the people
of the United States entirely satisfied with their courts and the decisions of them? Is there not a great deal of agitation there for a change?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think
so. But the Supreme Court of the United States settled the question of slavery after the war; the action of Abraham Lincoln was upheld by the decision of the court. But even if there are disputes there, so are there disputes here, and it is for us to make the system perfect as far as possible. Personally I will trust Canadian judges any day for the final decision, and especially the Supreme Court when we have strengthened it. And to my mind Canadian lawyers are absolutely the best men to interpret the laws of Canada.
There is only one other question I desire to speak to and that is the question as to the demand for a merger of our railway systems in this country. Things cannot go on as they have done in the past. We have been rolling up a huge snowball of liabilities ii. connection with our National Railways, and the Canadian Pacific has also been meeting tremendous expenditures. Unless we do something to put a stop to the enormous waste which is taking place in connection with the Canadian National Railways, I cannot see anything ahead but disaster; and the only solution, as I have said before, lies in a merger of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National system. This I know is objected to by a good many newspapers, particularly in Montreal, where probably a chain of journals are opposed to it. It does seem to me however that the country is behind the proposal for the consolidation of the two railway systems as the only means of eliminating unnecessary competition and putting an end to wasteful and extravagant expenditures. If these two roads were consolidated to-morrow,

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (York)
I would venture the prediction that the joint income, as a result of the savings that would be effected, would meet the liability in regard to dividends in connection with Canadian Pacific, and the merger would in my opinion prove entirely successful. We should then have a railway system that would really pay its way, instead of operating a huge company, not altogether to the advantage of the shareholders in the case of the Canadian Pacific, and not to the benefit of the public in the case of the National. system. The shareholders of the Canadian Pacific can no more stand competition than can those of any other railway system. I am sure the shareholders of this railway are not quite certain as to whether their 10 per cent dividend can last under this competition. As to the proposal itself, it was not even considered by some of the newspapers, not even by the Montreal Star. It was however intimated that it would be desirable to cut out the un-
10 p.m. necessary competition, and some of the press have been shouting in that respect. But they do not want to see any merger brought about. Now, competition will not be eliminated in any other way; there must be an absolute merging of the two lines if the full benefits of the elimination of competition are to be enjoyed.
Talking about the merging of railways, I might refer the House to what is going on in the United States. Hundreds of railways in that country were exploited to a marvellous degree by the men who controlled them, and the United States government has issued an order to the Interstate Commerce Commission to the effect that they compel all railways in that country to be merged into probably seven or eight systems. This will mean the wiping out of millions and millions of securities that were put out by those who have exploited these roads; and the Interstate Commerce Commission has further ordered that all these railroads, when they are merged, shall operate and take profits on a valuation made by expert actuaries on the actual values in the roads and not the capital issued. The same thing will come in this country unless we stop the rivalry that now exists between the two systems here. All that need be done is for the two roads to get together and take care of all the securities that are out; this would eliminate the waste that is now incurred through unnecessary competition. Just imagine two great headquarters in Montreal with two managing staffs, hundreds of offices and hundreds of men, where half the staffs, half the men and half the chief officers might serve equally well. This would mean an enormous saving.

speechtext:
Would the same theory
apply to the merging of the banking institutions?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it would not; does the hon. member want to have the banks merged into one? Be that as it may, a merger of the railways in this country would solve our difficulties.
I might mention what has been done by the Northwestern Railway Company in England. That concern has issued a statement to the effect that its expenses must be reduced owing to competition. And they have not been extravfagant either. What happened in England has happened in Canada as well, and it is this: the automobile and the motor truck have taken away a good deal of the local business of our railways. Take for instance the city of Toronto. If a man buys a carload of manufactured goods he simply gives his order over the telephone; a motor truck will take a load of from three to five tons from Kitchener and deliver it in Toronto six hours after, unloading it there, and there will be no cartage nor railway freight. The automobile business has therefore seriously affected the profits of our railways. And the railways are menaced from another quarter in this country: the United States and Canada intend developing the St. Lawrence waterway, and that will cut into the profits of the railway systems. Still more are the railways threatened in their high class business, such as express and passenger services, by the aeroplane, which within three years will be all over America. The Canadian Pacific Railway, then, ought to pray God every night to be taken over by the Canadian National system so that its shareholders might be assured for some time to come of the dividends or a portion of the dividends they now receive. Instead of these railways fighting for business they should get together to stop the over-competition that now exists. I will close by reading an extract from an editorial I have received in the mail. This editorial is reprinted from the Border Cities Star, published in Essex, which is represented in this House at the present time by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), and by the successor of a former member of this House, the late Hon. Mr. Kennedy. It is under the caption, "Duplications,' and I quote from it the following:
Mr. W. F. Maclean, M.P., has been commended for calling attention to expensive duplication of certain services at Ottawa. Mr. Maclean deserves commendation for he has placed his finger upon a condition that is almost criminal in its extravagance. Let us hope that he keeps on complaining and that his protests may not fall upon deaf ears forever.



The Budget-Mr. Maclean (York)
Mr. Maclean is also interested in eliminating another form of duplicated service-that of railways. He desires the. Canadian National to take over the Canadian Pacific so that great economies may be secured and the whole Dominion transportation problem straightened out. An ambitious thought, this, but one that is not likely to be worked out for the very good reason that the Canadian Pacific Railway is not anxious to be taken over and the business interests of the country are not keen on publicly-owned railroads anyway. Mr. Maclean may find it necessary to turn his argument around, that is to advocate the taking over of the Canadian National by the Canadian Pacific.
I want to tell you why I oppose that proposal. The Canadian National is owned by the people of Canada; the Canadian Pacific is owned about one-third in Canada, one-third in the United States and one-third in Great Britain. The control of that railway could be bought any day by English capitalists who went after it, or toy the New York Central or the Pennsylvania system of the United States. They could buy the Canadian Pacific tomorrow-and they may be after it; but they could not buy the Canadian National railways because they are owned by the people of this country. So I resent this doctrine propounded in the Border Cities Star. Yet this western writer admits the whole case when he says:
That there is an urgent need for the building of additional branch lines in the west is known to everyone familiar with that part of Canada. At the same time, there is a natural hesitancy to pass appropriations for such work for the simple reason that our present railway bills are so high. With amalgamation of the two great national systems, the saving of millions in expenses annually, and the lifting of the load that now reposes on the shoulders of the people, there would be money, opportunity and desire to proceed with those vital branch extensions.
The Border Cities Star favours the consolidation of the roads, but under the Canadian Pacific. I am against that; I am in favour of the consolidation of ;the roads under the Canadian National, which is owned by the people and which has sixty or seventy per cent of the railway strategy of Canada. I mean this: the old Grand Trunk was the greatest railroad system ever built on this continent. It got all the strategy at Montreal. It got all the strategy along lake Ontario, of the city of Toronto, of the Niagara district, of the Detroit river, to say nothing of a great many other portions of Ontario. The Canadian National has the strategical advantage in respect to the passes through the Rocky mountains and in the matter of grades. The Canadian Pacific has been made a great road by the contribution of the people of Canada, but we do not own it. I say we do own the Canadian National, and we must take care of it. When we consider the reduction in business and the increased competition involved in the waterway routes of
fMr. W. F. Maclean.]	>
the St. Lawrence we have got to get down to the cold-blooded business of doing something to merge these roads and eliminate unnecessary competition.
The farmers of the west see that things are improving for them; the prospects are that conditions will be better in that part of the country. Nobody wants to see the west go ahead more than I do. Some people say the representatives of the west are a class here, but what are we in the east but a class? They have as much right to be here and to state their cases as we have. From what some people say you would almost think they were bolsheviks, intruders; but the farmers of the west are Canadian citizens who elect their members to parliament and they have as much right to express their opinion here as anybody eJae Personally I speak here for 120,000 people whom I represent, many of whom are engaged in industries in my riding; rvho believe in diversity of employment and who want to see work provided for their own people. They believe, as I do, that extravagance of all kinds should cease. I want the Acting Minister of Finance to say to-day whether he approves of the unnecessary expenditure involved in the duplex system we have in this House, to which I referred on a previous occasion-two systems of post offices, two systems of messengers, and all the rest of it. Here is where economy could be practised, and the country demands it. When we begin to work it out in our own House then we can work it out in the country. Let us put an end to this unnecessary competition between the railways and thus make things better both for the railways themselves and for the country. Let us still have some respect for the principles that underlie that old, much denounced idea of a National Policy in this country for the encouragement of home industry, for the providing of employment for our own working people, for the maintaining of a home market for our own products.. Speaking particularly for the people whom I represent in this House, I say to-day that we do not want to see that National Policy abolished at this time, after the Great war and after the great losses in life and in money that our country has sustained.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the somewhat
lengthy discussion which has already taken place it is perhaps not necessary for me to say very much with regard to the details of the budget. We are told that there is no deficit; yet on the other hand we must con-

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
fess that we have decreasing revenues and increasing obligations. Just how long this state of affairs can continue is a matter that surely ought to call for the most serious consideration from this House. I submit that increased revenues can in the long run be secured only on the basis of general prosperity. To-day without doubt we have low wages, unemployed workers, idle factories, and discouraged farmers. Under these circumstances how can we hope for any immediate change in the situation in the near future? And in this respect I am not thinking particularly of one party or the other; I think both parties are in the grip of the larger economic forces over which politicians have very little control indeed.
We hear a great deal about the necessity for greater economy, but I would urge that this economy is not to be gained simply by petty retrenchment, although this may be desirable. Certainly it is not to be gained by any reduction in the necessary services which the country is rendering. In all fairness to the government, I think it should be recognized that the greater part of the budget is uncontrollable, that is, it consists of fixed charges, very largely interest charges. On the other hand, it does seem to me as if the government should very frankly face the enormous debt and should take steps, as I think was suggested by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) this afternoon, to deal with this war debt. I do not know that I agree with his suggestion of a sinking fund; it seems to me that this would not be adequate to meet the needs of the country; but I do believe we will not get very far towards alleviating our taxation until we tackle the war debt. Earlier in the session I called attention to the fact that if we add together the federal, provincial and municipal expenditures on the basis of nine million people, we have an annual expenditure of $89 per bead. I do not think that at the present moment we have nine million of a population. So that, roughly speaking, we have a per capita expenditure of $100. Think what that means to an ordinary family of five-$500 per annum! As to the war debt, if we add together the federal, provincial and municipal debt we get a per capita debt of $547-an enormous load for our people to carry. It should also be remembered that the debt is owed to a considerable extent to people resident in Canada, which means that a comparatively small group who hold the debt are able to levy tribute of some one hundred million dollars a year on the rest of the Canadian people. That is, that amount 147i
is being paid to Canadian bondholders; and over half that amount is in untaxable bonds. As long as that condition of affairs continues we are bound to have very heavy taxation. Sometimes I have wondered just what would happen if we adopted the old Mosaic law and every fifty years instituted a year of jubilee under which all slaves and debtors would go free. I am not very sure that a very large proportion of our population would suffer very much if we had such a jubilee. I do know that it would be a wonderful relief to industry if these enormous overhead charges could be rolled off.
Now I pass to a consideration of our National railways, for we all recognize that they are the source of a very considerable part of the deficits which come to us from year to year, whether those deficits are formally recognized by the government or not. I take it that we are undoubtedly committed to the principle of government ownership; there is no going backward, we must go forward. Sometimes the impression is given that we are in difficulties over the Canadian National because of the very high wages paid to labour Let me say that in 1920 there were 185,177 employees receiving $290,510,518. I am speaking now of railway employees as a whole. In 1921 the railway employees of Canada, numbering 167,627, were receiving $247,756,138; in 1922, 165,635 railway employees were receiving $233,294,040; in 1923, 178,052 employees were receiving $253,320,005; in 1924, 159,030 employees were receiving $231,517,862. I might say that the latter figures are hardly complete ; they are the latest available but include only the operating departments. Now, the higher salaries account for a considerable portion of the expenditures on wages and salaries. The salaries of the general officers amount to a little less than five million dollars a year. In 1923 the general office superintendence class numbered only 20,828. I would point out that although there has been a bigger volume of trade, this increased business has been handled at less expense. I note in the Canadian National Railways operating expenses that, although there was an increase in the salaries and expenses of the general officers from 1892, when it was $693,271.03, to 1923, when it amounted to $947,576.89, the payroll of the operating departments was cut by $7,714,263. Thus, although the higher officials have increased the expense in connection with the whole operation, wages have been steadily cut notwithstanding the larger volume of business handled.
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

There is another point to which I should like to draw attention; it has come up again and again in this House, and so far no action has been taken towards remedying the unsatisfactory condition. That is the overcapitalization of our railways, and I want to speak especially as to how this affects wages, or may react on wages. In this respect I think I cannot do better than read a few paragraphs from an article which appeared in the February number of the Canadian Railroad Employees' Monthly:

The C.P.R. with a total mileage of 19,103 has a capitalization of $623,960,000, or about $32,800 per mile. The C.N.R. with a total mileage of 26,751 has a capitalization of $2,207,000,000, or $84,500 per mile. The capitalization of the Canadian National system is made up as follows:

the public domain nearly equal to the area of the three Maritime provinces was thus turned over to railway promoters and their political friends. More than half of this great area was presented to the C.P.R. and its subsidiaries, that company on most of its main lines being permitted to make selections of the land likely to prove the most valuable. When the Grand Trunk Pacific was projected the policy of making large land grants was discontinued, and that road only obtained 11,800 acres from the Dominion government.
In addition the Dominion, provincial, and municipal governments gave cash subsidies to the private railways to the amount of $230,000^00 and guaranteed railway bonds to the tune of $442,000,000. The high .capitalization of the Canadian government railways {Which includes the old Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Hudson Bay railways) is partly explainable by the fact that they did not receive cash subsidies or land grants. Again, successive deficits have been added to their capital liabilities.
To the old I.C.R. capital account, too, was charged the construction of important harbour works at St. John and Halifax, whereas the C.P.R. and Grand 
Trunk have had the benefit of fine port facilit* *s at Montreal with little capital outlay in that conm ction. If the government roads had been credited with subsidies and land grants equivalent to those given other roads, their capitalization would have presented a different figure.
The old Intercolonial itself only represents a capital investment of $120,220,000 according to the public ^accounts of Canada for 1923 (schedule F. to balance sheet). But in the great railway building age the politicians in the east as well as the west got charters and subsidies to build small branch lines to open up forest areas or mining districts. Then when these lines had served the purpose of stripping the more acceptable and valuable timber areas, they, in many cases, managed to persuade the government to buy the line and add it to the government system. There was much log-rolling in those days. And thus in the construction of the government system its capitalization was augmented by practices, legal enough perhaps, but hardly justifiable from a moral point of view. The railway history of Canada is replete with stories of railway promoters amassing snug fortunes, for which they rendered no adequate service to the country.
It is scarcely fair-
And this is the point I should like to press in this connection and the reason for reading these figures-
-that the burdens of the sins of the politicians and the promoters should be visited upon the railway workers to the third and fourth generations.

The sum of these accounts is $1,581,000,000, and that is the sum on which the Canadian National Railway is expected to pay interest, a matter of nearly $75,000,000 per year. I will not go into this question in detail; it simply suggests a line of reasoning which I am glad to say, is very frequently met with across this country; and I am very sure that if the government could see its way to write off some of this over-capitalization as simply bad debts we would be in a very much better position to carry forward our national lines to success.
There is just one other point I should like to mention in connection with the railway situation, and in doing so to take my place beside the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) who has been a veteran advocate of public ownership. In the first session of this parliament I can remember advocating the unification of our two-company system. At that time the whole idea was regarded as absolutely impracticable, and apparently there was no use in urging it upon the House. I am glad to think in the last four years we have come a few steps nearer that veTy desirable development; and this year when the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr Euler) came to the support of the hon. member for South York, I am sure that we all felt that perhaps the time might not be so remote as some of us imagined, when this unification would take place, and place us in a fair way towards the solution of one of the most important problems which confront us in Canada to-day.
With regard to the question of free trade and protection, the discussion of which has occupied so much time up to the present, I might say that the labour movement does not regard this as by any means a fundamental issue. Later in the discussion I should like to deal with some aspects of this question a little more fully, but at this time perhaps I might be permitted to comment very briefly
upon a few of the arguments which have been advanced. A year ago we found the government making a great deal of the fact that it was granting certain reductions on agricultural implements. We have had from the opposition a great deal of criticism and the supposed adverse effects of these reductions have been pointed out. I think one hon. member has already referred to some statistics as to what these reductions really amount to. I hope that some of the Progressive members will take this matter up more fully. I shall content myself at this stage with calling attention to the bare facts of the case. On imports of all dutiable agricultural implements valued at $3,156,986, April 1 to October 31, 1924, there was a reduction of 4.7 per cent or an actual reduction of duty paid by the farmers of the whole of Canada of $148,378. Dividing that amount by the acres in field crops we find that the saving to the farmer amounted to only 83 cents per half section.

speechtext:
These figures were for the acres in field crops.
The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) the financial critic of the opposition, made quite a bid for labour sup-

port in his speech advocating protection. In the course of his speech he stated that prices of manufactured products to consumers embody labour costs equal to 60 per cent, and in some cases 80 per cent of such prices. The inference would seem to be that under protection high enough Canada would manufacture $700,000,000 worth of goods now imported, and pay labour 60 to 80 per cent of that amount.
Now, according to the Bureau of Statistics for 1922, at the point of production the gross value of Canada's manufactured products was $2,439,000,000. The combined salaries and wages amounted to $497,800,000. The ratio of salaries and wages at factory valuation was therefore 20.2 per cent; the factory value of a hundred dollars, plus wholesaler and retailer and transportation, would make the consumer's price anything above $130. Assume the average consumer's price is $140, which would be very conservative, then the factory labour cost would be $140 divided by 20.2 or 14.3 per cent, instead of 60 or 80 per cent. I might call attention to the fact that in many industries labour costs form a very much smvalleT proportion than this. In the flour mills they represent something like 3 per cent of the consumers' flour prices. If we cut out salaries, the average wage labour costs of all manufactured products would be about 11 per cent of the consumer's price. Of course, labour costs are embodied in raw material, but the producer of raw materials in Canada would have the same wage bill whether the raw materials are manufactured in Canada or elsewhere. Similarly, consumer's prices embody wage bills of transportation companies and merchants; but from the wage point of view, whether they handle Canadian or foreign manufactured articles is immaterial. The statements of the hon. member for West York refer only to factory labour costs. I would say that, in view of these considerations, decidedly they are not convincing. Further than that, the hon. member for West York rather gave us the impression that our salvation economically would be along the lines of following France. It is most unfortunate for him that the recent developments in France took place so very soon after his speech was made. I think I cannot do better than quote from an editorial which appeared in the issue of the Grain Growers' Guide of April 15:
Fairness to France demands recognition of the vast outlay she has had to make for the restoration of the devastated districts, but if comparisons of national welfare are to be made it is also necessary to recognize that the outlay has been by way of currency inflation, and to such an extent that the franc has depreciated

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
74 per cent. The financial position of the country now is such that the government of M. Herriot is staking its life on a financial proposal involving the issue of two billions of currency, and a forced loan of 100,000,000,000 francs for 10 years at 2 or 3 per cent. The currency issue is necessary to meet issues of the Bank of France in excess of those already authorized by law, and it is stated that these unauthorized issues of the bank have been concealed from the people.
On her foreign debt France is paying neither interest nor principal, and it is very questionable whether the French war debts will ever be redeemed. France, as Sir George Paish stated in his recent speech in Winnipeg, is on the verge of bankruptcy, and if the inflation continues it will mean the complete wiping out of the internal debt. Protection has nothing whatever to do with the condition in France; if anything it is making a bad situation much worse.
I take it that we should be very careful in making comparisons between two countries that differ so very widely in their general economic development as do France and Canada.

speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
turn to page 1998 of Hansard he will find what I said. I criticized the hon. member for East Calgary for saying that "combines cannot be broken, and even if they could be broken, it would be very bad business." I said that was rank heresy so far as I understood the claims of organized labour.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is what I am
trying to say. That is the statement I wish to discuss. Let me say this much in defence, if necessary, and explanation of the position taken by my colleague. He had said that combines are the natural outcome of the processes which had1 been going on for the last century. He had been showing that we had long since passed beyond the stage of unrestricted competition, unrestricted free trade. He showed that in that sense combines really represented progress; that they were inevitable. He says further:
I have been suggesting, not the breaking of a combine but the control of a definite monopoly in Canada.
And he went on further to say in another place:

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
The control of a world combine is only possible by a world force.
All I should like ito call attention to is that the words against which the criticism was levelled, if taken by themselves, might readily be regarded as making my colleague justify combines as they exist, and might suggest that he would leave them alone with all their evils, whereas he wtas simply showing that we cannot do away with combines buit that we should control them. That is altogether a different matter. I wanted to make it clear to the House that this is what my colleague and I stand for.
The Minister of Labour also took issue with the member for East Calgary regarding a particular case of an immigrant who came to this country and who was out of work. A letter was read in the House from the immigrant. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) took the trouble to make an investigation and read a somewhat lengthy statement according to which this immigrant was a very unworthy character. I may say that the statements made in the memorandum submitted by the Minister of Labour have been definitely denied by the man in question but I have no way of determining whose statement is correct, that of the Minister of Labour or that of the immigrant. But it does not in the slightest degree matter, for the purposes of the argument which my colleague was making, which was simply this, that the government had evidently brought out people who were not satisfactorily located on the land. That was the argument, and this particular case was merely incidental. I call attention to the matter in passing.
Now a few remarks with regard to the question of free trade and protection. I think the hon. member for West York was quite correct when he pointed out that there no longer existed in this country the conditions which would seem to afford ground for the belief that free trade as such would offer a solution to our modem problems. The conditions have absolutely changed since the old days when there was unrestricted free trade between individuals. We are living to-day in the age of trusts and combines of various kinds and as a matter of fact we have no longer the kind of free trade that existed in the days when this fiscal doctrine 'became popular through the Manchester school of economics. In Great Britain protection was the policy of the land-owners who wished to keep out agricultural products and other raw materials which were produced in England. This became the political gospel of the Conservative party, which was the party

of the land-owners. Free trade on the other hand was the political gospel of the trading and manufacturing classes of Great Britain and became the recognized policy of the Liberal party, which was very largely the party of the traders and manufacturers. We are often accused these days of advocating something new in suggesting group representation in parliament. The two old historical parties originally represented distinct groups in England, one the group of landed proprietors and the other the group of traders and manufacturers. In Canada the situation has been quite different; protection in Canada has been the policy of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and of whatever party happens to be in power, while free trade has been to a considerable extent the policy of the agriculturists. To-day there is really no such thing as individual competition. We may still have the competition of rival groups, those 'groups are sometimes located in a single country, sometimes in different countries, in which case the rivalry tends to become an international dispute. We see on all sides the emergence of these huge trusts, and this development entirely alters the situation and should alter our attitude towards the whole problem. I remember a very interesting treatment of, the question of the tariff from the standpoint of the restriction of production. I read a paragraph from a little pamphlet On the Nature and Uses of Sabotage by Professor Thorstein Veblen:
The great standing illustration of sabotage administered by the government is the protective tariff, of course. It protects certain special interests by obstructing competition from beyond the frontier. This is the main use of a national boundary. The effect of the tariff is to keep the supply of goods down and thereby keep the price up, and so to bring reasonably satisfactory dividends to those special interests which deal in the protected articles of trade, at the cost of the underlying community. A protective tariff is a typical conspiracy in restraint of trade. It brings a relatively small, though absolutely large, run of free income to the special interests which benefit by it, at a relatively, and absolutely, large cost to the underlying community, and so it gives rise to a body of vested rights and intangible assets belonging to these special interests.
I	suggest that the economic developments of recent years are rendering the older political divisions obsolete. These great industrial,
commercial and financial concerns
II	p.m. reach across our international
boundaries and we can no longer carry on the affairs of any one country as if we were or could be self-contained in our business activities. Let me put it this way: Capital is international; why therefore should we attempt to make industry and commerce hational? I should like to have that question answered by some hon. gentleman. Let

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
me emphasize it. Capital itself has become international, and capital is recognized as the great driving force, superior to either the commercial power or the industrial power of to-day. Capital is international; why should we attempt to make industry or commerce national? To do so is to attempt the impossible. The labour solution lies neither in the direction of free trade, which under present conditions is not possible, nor in the direction of protection, which so far has meant the protection of industry and not the protection of the worker. I can conceive of there being developed an altogether new kind of protection, a protection not of industries but of standards of living. That would place the matter on a different basis. In our labour unions we frequently make use of the union label which placed on goods guarantees that they have been produced under fair and reasonable conditions with regard to hours, working conditions, and wages. I would suggest that we might apply that principle in the larger field and insist that all goods should be produced under standards of living that measure up to a certain level. For that reason we in the labour	movement are interested in the
maintenance of the standards in Europe. We are interested in raising the standards in the Orient. If we are to have goods imported from Germany or other parts of Europe where their standards have been forced down since the war we will inevitably have our standards here forced down, and in some way we should be protected from goods of that character. If we are to have huge quantities of goods shipped in from the Orient where their standards have never been as high as our standards, we will meet with difficulties; we will be ousted in this country. It is no solution simply to say, "exclude the orientals;" we need to go further and see that the standards in the Orient are raised. The British Labour party has been dealing with this matter in recent weeks.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask how the goods in this country are to be protected, if cheap German or other goods are not wanted here?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was just coming
to that point. The British Labour party has been facing that in the importation of large quantities of German goods in recent times. A good deal of pressure has been brought to bear from the Conservative section of the British parliament. On March 17, for example, in the British House a Conservative resolution was presented declaring that free import of goods produced under sweated conditions was inconsistent with the principles
of British trade unionism. Now, that argument, presented by a Conservative, was answered from the Labour standpoint. I have not been able yet to read that copy of the Hansard, but a similar position was taken a little earlier. On February 16 a debate took place in the House on a motion submitted by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald declaring that the policy of the government with regard to the safeguarding of industries and the methods by which it was proposed to carry this policy into effect must lead to a system of general tariffs which would not enlarge the volume of trade and safeguard the interests of workers as regards employment, wages and conditions. In the course of that debate Mr. MacDonald asked:
Would not the government instead of trying to put up a wall against "sweated" goods that experience showed could never be fully effective, take steps to eliminate "sweated" goods altogether, bo that they would not be available either for home or for foreign consumption?
In the International Labour Office-
Mr. MacDonald said:
-they had an instrument for co-ordinating labour conditions in all industrial countries, but he would be very much surprised if the Conservative government and the Conservative party had recently "lifted a little finger to increase the authority of the International Labour Office in order to raise the status of labour throughout Europe."
Undoubtedly we should extend and strengthen the conventions of the Washington conference following the principles laid down by the Versailles treaty, and should insist that we should not have dumped on us goods that came to us from countries which maintain a low standard of living, and refuse to ratify those conventions. I may say that the only practical objection to this policy lies in the fact that Canada herself has not ratified most of those Washington conventions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
think it possible to figure out what countries have the low standards ol living to which he refers? Can you make a general rule applicable to any nation like France or Germany, or does not the cost of living enter into it as well?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course, but if we had the eight-hour day, for example, as a world condition; if we had proper conditions of work applying the world over; if certain minimum requirements were insisted upon all along the line, I would say that if our boasted superiority means anything we should be able to compete with the people of other countries. If not, we sihall go down and I am sure we shall deserve it.

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is there any nation which has these conditions to which my hon. friend refers-the eight-hour day and so on?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A number of
nations have already ratified those conventions. If the hon. gentleman cares to read the document from which I am quoting-Industrial and Labour Information as published at Geneva by the International Labour Office, he will find a record of the ratifications made by the various nations. It is very gratifying tc find how many of them have been ratified, but it is not very creditable to Canada that so few of them have 'been ratified by Canada. Our practical difficulty in urging this policy might very well be that other nations that have already ratified these conventions might boycott our goods because they are produced under sweated conditions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Talking about the subject of protection with relation to working conditions generally, is it not true that some years ago the low-paid workmen of India, who had a very low standard of living, asked for protection in order to keep out English manufactured goods, made by workmen at higher wages and with a very much higher standard of living?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And working the eight-hour day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I believe that is
so, and I have every confidence that if the conditions of labour are what they should be, this will prove to be of immense advantage to the industry. It has 'been clearly demonstrated, I think, that from the standpoint of output the eight-hour day is better than the ten or twelve-hour day; that reasonable standards of living and working conditions are at least as effective as the slave-driving that sometimes has been prevalent in our factories. Decent treatment of the workers is surely good business. I throw this out. I simply call attention to this constructive suggestion which has come to us from the British labour movement as it seems to me to be quite practicable. It may be necessary for us in this country to adopt some measure of protection for the workers-protection, I say, not of the industry in order that it may profit by special privileges, but protection against goods that may be manufactured under low grade conditions and by sweated labour.
Just in passing I would say that one of the worst features of the present Dawes plan is that it would seem definitely to lower the

conditions of the German workers, reducing them to a position very little short of industrial serfdom. If that takes place we may rest assured that the condition will be reflected here in Canada, as we shall have to come into competition with goods manufactured under those conditions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But in the long run,
would the hon. member not think that goods produced under wholesome conditions would be produced cheaper than under unwholesome conditions?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think so, because in the long run the general intelligence of the people would more than counteract any supposed advantage resulting from the production under unwholesome conditions. It is just a question of time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why, then, should we need to protect ourselves against these poorly paid workmen?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, there is the
immediate effect, and this might become a permanent condition if there is an almost unending supply of cheap labour. Men will become prematurely worn out between thirty and forty years of age and allow fresh workers to take their place. Thus an abundant supply of workers might carry on by mere brute force. I do not believe that ultimately people of lower standards are going to ride over us, but in the meantime I say it may be necessary to afford protection for our workers. As a matter of fact, nearly all our professions, as well as our labour unions, are built up on the principle of protection. My friend from Brome (Mr. MoMaster) belongs to one of the most highly protected unions in Canada-the lawyers' union. I am quite confident that he and his fellow practitioners would be well able to hold their place with the whole world in interpreting the law, certainly with those of us who are mere laymen and still the lawyers think it is necessary to maintain certain standards to protect their profession.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To protect the public
against irresponsible practitioners.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The medical profession in the same way say, "We need to protect the public."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about preachers?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I presume preachers would be in the same class, and as far as I know school teachers are also. Theoretically, undoubtedly in the long run, innate intelligence-shall I say?

and the general intel-

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
Ieetual level of the country will tell. But I think we are all agreed that a certain measure of protection might possibly be necessary to meet special conditions. I should like to say to my hon. friend from Brome, who has put forward this question, that we have passed-absolutely passed-the stage when free trade can be offered as a solution, because the conditions which lay behind the doctrine of free trade have long since been passed by in the development of industry.
Mr. COOTE^ Can the hon. member suggest any way by which we can protect the wheat producers of this country against the cheap labour of India, one of the competing countries against us in the export markets of the world?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is the very
problem I have in view when I urge that we must face the fact of world competition. In my judgment we must advocate, as the only ultimate solution, the raising of the standards even of the so-called backward races. It will take some time. For a while we may retain our lead because of superior advantages in the country itself, superior educational facilities, and so on, but sooner or later we shall have to face the fact that the world is a unit and that no part can retain a low standard without its adversely affecting the other parts.
With regard to the motion now before the House, Mr. Speaker, we shall be inclined to support. the amendment, because we believe that in one respect at 'least this very carefully drawn amendment, which does not go very far-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And is quite self-contradictory.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be in some
respects, but at least it does call attention to one of the evils, the sales tax, and in a general way it advocates economy, which is a good thing, only as I have said we ought to go much further than these petty economies to which referencei is often made. It may be difficult for us to decide how to vote on the amendment but we shall vote without any hesitation against the budget, because it does not offer any solution whatever to problems which face us to-day. Now I should like to pass to another topic altogether, that is-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the hon. gentleman
leaves his theory of protection, he will understand that any policy which eoulld be adopted by this House would have to be a general policy, it would have to cover the wheat
producer as well as the working man. Could he define just a little more clearly how his theory would apply to the wheat producer, as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) tried to elicit, because it is important?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think I
have anything further to add to what . I have already said. I was simply suggesting this as a principle that we might attempt to work out. If there are countries producing wheat where the standards are very low, we might refuse to trade with those countries.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They would not be
shipping wheat in here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But we are shipping things to them, and we could use a certain amount of pressure, because if we want to ship wheat out we must get something else back in return. We must constantly remember that every export must be balanced by an import, and I take it that even the threat to boycott any country because of its low standards will have a very material effect in enabling that country to raise its standards. I am just giving the general principle. I know it opens a large field, and I have no idea of being dogmatic; I am merely suggesting a possible line of advance.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
permit me a question? He says that we ship large quantities of things to these low priced, sweated labour countries that are producing goods under conditions adverse to labour. we to fear?

speechtext:
I simply repeat
what I have said before, that temporarily we may have to fear them because of their great mass of human labour and their low standards under which labour can be simply poured into their productive machine without any thought as to the effect on the labour itself. I might point out however that

it was not until the sanitary conditions of the zone were improved that they were able to put the canal through.

conditions?

speechtext:
Might I point out that
the raising of the standard of living of the farmers of India, for instance, and the raising of their general standard of intelligence as well, would mean that they would be producing with more efficient machinery than they are using to-day. They are threshing their grain by driving their oxen over it; we thresh it by very efficient machinery. Consequently we are able to produce wheat cheaper and compete with them on the export markets of the world.

And they probably
gamer their wheat with a sickle.

A large question is raised there, Mr. Speaker, which I think it would not be wise to enter upon at present. Now I propose to pass to the discussion of the coal situation, but I see it is already very late, nearly half past eleven, and I should like very much, if the House would permit me, Mr. Speaker, to adjourn the debate.

I feel that I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without referring to a matter which is in the minds of a great many of us at the present time, the situation in Cape Breton. May I again call the attention of the House to the history of this company which is again asking for special favours. According to Poor and Moody's Manual Consolidated 1922, at the merger of the British Empire Steel Corporation the total issues of component companies were:	[DOT]
Common	$ 63,000,000
Preferred	 19,000,000

At the merger the old issues were increased and transmuted thus
Common	$ 24,000,000

Thus water is turned into wine. A fact finding commission would disclose whether the preferred or common stock represents any equity 'behind the funded debt or whether all such issues went to promoters, exploiters, legislators, and bondholders as bonus.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Have you got the
