subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me call attention to this: the Annual Financial Review -Canadian-of June, 1923, has evidence that the Nova Scotia legislature authorized Besco to issue $500,000,000 in capital stock. I find on page 181 of this Review with regard to the reduction of capital:
That the president moved as a special resolution of the shareholders of the corporation:
"That the capital of the company be reduced from $500,000,000 to $250,000,000,"
In this connection I might read the following quotation from an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of July 29, 1924:
There has been issued in addition to the foregoing $101,750,000 and so far as evidence appears in this regard, this amount appears to have been entirely in the nature of a bonus distribution to the bondholders and the parties promoting the merger.
Now, the miners themselves have been trying to express their view with regard to this proposed bonus, and in view of the history of the corporation I should like to present the miners' own view in this connec-

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
tion. I find in the Labour Herald of March 7, this statement:
McLurg was asked: "If the miners accept a reduction in their wages, will the company reduce the selling price of coal to the consumer?" His reply was "No, we require the money for our bondholders and shareholders."
According to that statement even although the miners were forced ultimately to accept a reduction in wages it will not mean one cent of benefit to the consumers but simply an added profit to the company on distribution to the bondholders. The article continues:
Their annual statement shows that they paid out in dividends for the five year periods ending 1921 on preferred shares $5,350,000, and on common shares $7,786,376.12. They also laid away in reserve funds $9,500,000. Since then they got from the Dominion government $4,500,000 for a plate mill they erected. They own both the mill and the money now.
In the last issue of the Canadian Railway Employees' Monthly is an article by Mr. J. B. McLachlan, the editor of the Glace Bay Herald from Which I take the following statement:
Besco was organized in the year 1920, for the primary purpose of eliminating all duplication of production costs then existing because of independent coal companies operating in the same areas. Besco has either cut down that cost, or it has not. The miners claim it has. It is a matter of record that the separate companies that existed before the merger did compete successfully in the Montreal market for two generations-and if the old companies with their greater overhead costs could do that, then Besco can do better under the more favourable conditions of the combine. Here is what Col. Thomas Cantley said on this point the other day when speaking of the ability of the old Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company to compete in the open markets previous to the Besco merger:
"From 1884 until December 31st, 1920, a period of 36 years, the Scotia Company earnings were $33,307,329.96 and as stated above, in only one year, 1897, was there any loss in operation and in that year the amount was trifling, being less than $5,000. The total dividends paid during the company's operations were $7,452,758.32-the balance of earnings being put back into the property."
Besco did cut out all duplication of production costs, and to-day is in a far better position than the old Nova Scotia companies to market coal in Montreal against all comers.
Then what is behind all this idleness and hunger? Are these just the results of a common industrial depression felt more or less everywhere? The game that Besco is playing is to secure a cut wage rate so that Besco can get cheaper coal for its steel works, its steamers, its ore mines, its lumber mills and for its boilers at its coal mines. The second phase of the game is to secure a higher tariff so that every other user of coal on the Atlantic sea-board from Sydney to Montreal shall pay more for their coal, and the idleness and hunger are the weapons being used to hold up the government and the country and the miners.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who writes this?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. J. B. McLachlan in the last number of the Canadian Railroad Employees' Monthly. In substantiation of this statement that the present merger ought to be aible to enter the Montreal market, Mr. McLachlan quotes from another statement, found on pages seven and eight of the annual statement of the Dominion Steel Corporation and constituent companies for the year ending March 31, 1921, as follows:
" In this connection," said Mr. Wolvin " I wish to call the attention of the holders of preferred shares to the fact that the statement for the fiscal year shows that dividends on your shares for the three companies named were earned five times over. I need not, of course, emphasize the fact that business is most unsatisfactory at present, and in view of this it is all the more gratifying to be able to say that for the first quarter of the current fiscal year ending June 30, the Dominion Steel Corporation after providing for depreciation, sinking fund, and bond interest, has earned at the rate of over three times the amount required for payment of the combined dividends on its preference shares, and on the preferred shares of its constituent companies."
The miners charge that Besco has deliberately refused to sell coal in the Montreal market during the past year, and has, and is, using the idleness and hunger of the miners as a means to cut the wages of producers and increase prices to consumers of coal. The miners in their misery are nothing more than pawns being used by Besco to force the hands of the government and the country. A ten per cent cut in the miners wages would net Besco annually an additional one and a half million dollars, an increased tariff will result in millions more for Besco out of the buyers of coal. By cheaper coal for its own concerns Besco would net at least another half million.
Nor do Besco's tariff delegations to Ottawa end with a mere tariff revision upwards. Here are some of the things that Besco also wants, before it can give the country and the miners any assurance that idleness and starvation shall end in Cape Breton: that the government subsidize coal converted into coke to take the place of anthracite; that the government increase the subvention on coal hauled on the railway, the subvention to aipply to sea-borne coal also; and that greater protection be given Canadian steel and steel products. In a word, Besco is holding up the country and trying to put across the biggest blackmailing scheme that this country has ever seen.
It is not merely the miners and the east who are protesting against the situation and asking that this government should do something.	I should like to read a few paragraphs from an editorial in the Winnipeg Evening Tribune of March 28, which discusses the proposed duty under the caption, " An incomplete solution." The editorial reads:
It is stated that the proposed increase in duty on American slack coal from 14 cents to 50 cents a ton offers a solution to the troubles of the Nova Scotia mining industry.
The article goes on:
Even if the proposed wage cut is not enforced and the present wage scale is continued, it will not compensate the miners for irregularities of employment, and even with more regular employment their condition would be none too good. Wages of coal miners in Nova Scotia are substantially lower than in
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

Alberta, for instance, as the following figures of daily wages published recently by the Department of Labour clearly show:
Alberta Nova Scotia
Contract miners (average)..	..	$8 33	$7	25Hand miners	
7	02	4	60Labourers underground	
6	03	3	65
No reasonably permanent solution of the industrial unrest in Nova Scotia can be hoped for until the workers, the lower paid ones especially, receive both higher wage rates and more regular employment.
Canadian public opinion will not be satisfied to let the present situation be smoothed over by the mere granting of a higher duty on imported coal. The British Empire Steel Corporation can hardly be said to enjoy the respect of the people of Canada. Proof is needed that the duty is really necessary.
I would like to impress this on my hon. friends on the other side:
Proof is needed that the duty is really necessary. It has been charged by the miners that the wages have been kept down in order that dividends might be paid on watered stock. If the increased duty is really necessary to enable Canadian coal operators to compete in Canada with American producers, the country has the right to know who is to benefit by that increased duty. Such facts can only be satisfactorily ascertained by a factfinding commission.
If the Dominion government has the legal right to impose 'a duty in the interests of a Nova Scotia industry it has an equal moral right to first institute a complete investigation as to whether that duty is necessary.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

I assume that you would expect, as a prime consideration of dealing with the Nova Scotia dispute that an investigation vrould be held to fix responsibility, and you should know that the federal government has no authority to go into Nova Scotia and summons one single individual before it to give evidence and to produce books, so that any attempt made by the federal government to carry on an investigation would be a simple farce, as the president and others connected with the British Empire Steel Corporation could simply decline to co-operate and to appear when summonsed or to produce books and documents.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

I quite agree with

The Privy Council decided in the Board of Commerce case that this federal government had no authority to make those inquiries into the cost of living. My hon. friend should read up the legal decisions in order to understand the position we are in. I -wish his view was correct and that we could do some of the things he wants. But we are
confronted with a reality, not a theory that the hon. member is talking about.

speechtext:
This parliament, by a
committee, did conduct an inquiry into the cost of living.

speechtext:
Exactly, but my hon.
friend will recall that after that was inquired into, when a somewhat similar matter was taken to the Privy Council the Privy Council decided that this federal government had no right to invade the "property and. civil rights" jurisdiction of the provinces.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Privy Council never decided anything of the kind.

speechtext:
The record speaks for
itself.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not so far as this parliamentary inquiry is concerned.

speechtext:
Perhaps the hon member
for Centre Winnipeg will proceed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are just two observations which I should like to make at this point. If conditions are really as they have been stated by members of the government, that is an excellent reason why we should abolish any appeal to the Privy Council. Further than that, I do not know of any greater service that I could render to the people of Canada to-night than to place before the public at large the attitude of the government in a crisis of this kind. I am quite willing to let the strictly legal aspects take care of themselves. The other day I came across a clipping with regard to the situation in Europe. This is an article by Rothay Reynolds in the Montreal Standard quoting from the great industrialist Herr Arnold Reoh-berg, the oil magnate. He said of conditions over there:
The captains of the coal and iron industries are more absolute masters of Germany than was William II.
I think we can almost say that of the captains of the coal and steel industry in Canada if the contentions of ministers of the crown are correct. I should like to ask: After all, who are these people that are holding up the country? We have talked about the responsibility of the government here and I think it has responsibility. We have talked about the responsibility of the government of Nova Scotia and I think it has responsibility. But I would say that the first responsibility lies immediately with the directors of this corporation. Who are they that thus defy the whole of the people of Canada? It is of interest that the people of
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

Canada should know this. Who are the directors of the British Empire Steel Corporation? They are:
R. M. Wolvin, President, Montreal, Que.; Major General Sir Newton J. Moore, K.C.M.G., VicePresident, London, Eng.; J. E. McLurg, Vice-President, Sydney, N.S.; Hon. C. P. Beaubien (Senator), Montreal, Que.; Sir Trevor Dawson, Bart., London, Eng.; Hector Maclnnes, K.C., Halifax, N.S.; W. D. Ross, Toronto, Ont.; J. F. M. Stewart, Toronto, Ont.; Galen L. Stone, Boston, Mass.; J. P. Middlesboro, Glasgow, Scot.; Right Hon. Lord Invemaim, Glasgow, Scot.; F. W. Ross, Quebec, Que.; Geo. F. Downs, New York, N.Y.; Hon. J. P. B. Casgrain (Senator), Montreal, Que; R. F. Hoyt, New York, N.Y.; Lome Webster (Senator), Montreal, Que.
I would note here that three of these directors are residents of Great Britain; three are residents of the United States; only two live [DOT]in the province of Nova Scotia. One of these is the company's attorney and, according to the papers, one of the men implicated in the bribery of the ex-premier of Newfoundland. Three of these men are senators, distinctly responsible at this crisis. I would say that all except the vice-president, Mr. McLurg, are absentee landlords. What is the spirit of McLurg, the vice-president? We have read bis words:
They cannot stand the gaff. We hold the cards. Let them stay out for six months. It matters not, eventually they .will come to us.
Here we have capitalism stark-naked and unashamed! That statement of McLurg's in future years, I have no doubt, will be placed side 'by side with that other characteristic statement of Mr. Paton, who was more truthful than some of the other captains of industry when he declared that "These mills were not built for the glory of God, but for the profits of the shareholders." These men hold in their power the destinies of large numbers of our fellow Canadians. This morning the relief authorities in the city of Ottawa received a telegram which states that to-day there are in Nova Scotia 27,200 individuals absolutely dependent upon the public for relief.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Might I re-, mind my hon. friend that Mr. Lewis, head of the United Mine Workers of America, has stated that that organization is financing the strikers?

speechtext:
Whatever may be
true of the future finances that may come from the United Mine Workers, I think we must accept the word of the relief agents who are absolutely disinterested and who only this morning sent this telegram to Ottawa:
Red Cross nurses report serious malnutrition. Local relief committee $11,000 in debt with the situation growing worse.

We cannot as a House pass by such a situation as that. Surely we have responsibility. The responsibility may rest primarily upon this board of directors whom I have named. There may be responsibility upon the labour organization over in the United States to come to the help of their comrades in Canada. But this federal government cannot escape the responsibility of taking action at this time. We have in our hands certain powers that, I think, will be admitted even by members of the government. We are proposing to grant still further concessions to this company at the very time that this outrage is being perpetrated. The least this government can do is absolutely to refuse further concessions until we have some settlement of this dispute along right lines.

speechtext:
, Does the hon. member
suppose that the change in the coal duties is responsible for the present strike?

speechtext: Is the hon. member not aware that there are a large number of independent coal companies in Nova Scotia outside the British Empire Steel Corporation? In my county there are three other companies operating.

speechtext:

that there are some other companies, mostly very small concerns, as the minister knows very well.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to pass now for a short time to another field. Sometimes Nova Scotia members ask us why we confine our investigations to the eastern coal fields and have little to say with regard to the west. I have tried on several occasions to call the attention of the House to the situation prevailing in Nova Scotia because it is more acute than the conditions obtaining elsewhere. But the situation in Alberta has recently been developing at so alarming a rate that I feel, even although the hour is late, since apparently it is not the wish that the matter should be carried over till to-morrow, that I should deal as briefly as I may with the larger aspect of the

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
situation as it affects the province of Alberta. First of all may I say to my farmer friends that perhaps they have not quite realized the importance of the coal industry in Canada; they have hardly realized how essential it is that this whole question of the development of our coal measures should be settled on some permanent basis. May I then quote a few statistics with regard to the general importance of the coal industry. In the first place, I should like to give the words of Mr. C. V. Corless with regard to agricultural areas. He says:
Adding together all these areas, suitable in surface, soil, and climate for profitable cultivation, including the cultivable valleys in the highlands, we find a total of rather less than 15 per cent of the area of Canada suitable for profitable agriculture. This leaves 85 per cent, of which the principal or only permanent basic industry is or will be mining. But fully one-third of even this agricultural part of Canada is known to be enormously rich in minerals.
Here now is a statement of the figures given by Dr. Dowling in the report of the Twelfth International Geological Congress. Referring to this, Mr. Corless says:
From the latter striking report, which is the best estimate yet made, I cull these startling figures for Canada's estimated total coal reserves.

This inconceivably large figure, 1,234 billions of tons roughly 35,000 times Canada's present total annual consumption, baffles the imagination. It is nearly sixty per cent greater than the total estimated reserves of the whole of Europe; nearly equal to those estimated for the whole of Asia; and one-sixth of those of the entire world.
I would urge that we should not continue to allow this vast natural inheritance of ours to be developed in any haphazard, wasteful, uneconomic way as we have done up to the present time, and that altogether aside from the unsatisfactory relations that have so far [DOT]existed between operators and employees. Many of you will recall the fact that a few years ago Great Britain made a serious investigation into the production of coal in that country, and we have the report of Mr. Justice Sankey which declared that-
Even upon the evidence already given the present system of ownership and working stands condemned and some other system must be substituted for it, either nationalization or a method of unification by .national purchase or by joint control.
When we hear so much about private ownership and vested interests it is well for us to read some of the evidence submitted before that very important commission. The replies given to the labour men, Mr. Smil'lie, Mr. 'Hodges and Sir Leo Money, are worth being pondered by the people in this country, where we have thought that vested interests have not secured so strong a foothold.
Now with regard to the Canadian situation, some of our mines are privately owned while others are under the control of 12 m. various provinces, and others again are in the control of the Dominion. Among these the chief field is in Alberta, and so I have a perfect right, I should take it, to bring this question before the federal House, inasmuch as the House has jurisdiction in the province of Alberta, at the present time, seeing that it controls the natural resources of that province. Now let me sketch very briefly the condition that prevails out there in the industry itself. I hold in my hand a list of the names of individuals and corporations who are recorded as the owners of coal mining rights acquired from the crown under the provisions of the coal mining regulations in the province of Alberta, and these individuals and corporations number 802, I have here also a list containing the names and addresses of individuals and corporations operating coal mining areas in the province of Alberta, numbering in the year 1923-the last figures available-353. We in the west hear a good deal of over-development, but I do not know of any figures that could: be more eloquent than this 353 as to coal development in Alberta.
Regarding the general position of the industry I quote from a memorandum prepared by the Coal Mining Lands branch of the Department of the Interior:
Coal mining rights were disposed of by sale up to the year 1907, and after that year by lease only. By an order in council dated the Oth May, 1907, the form of final title was changed from patent to lease Royalty at the prescribed rate is collected on all coal mined from lands acquired from the crown under the regulations since the 6th April, 1901, but no royalty is collected on the output of mines acquired prior to that date, and no returns of the operations of such mines are furnished the department, so that no information respecting the output of mines which were not acquired subject to the payment of royalty is obtained.
The output of coal mined from lands in the province of Alberta, acquired under lease from the crown during the calendar year 1924, was 1,694,172 tons, and the total output of coal during the same period from lands acquired by purchase under the regulations was 710,899 tons, making a total output of coal subject to the payment of royalty during the year 1924 of 2,405,071 These figures, however, do not include the quantity of coal mined from the 28,000 acres of coal mining lands

Just in passing may I also note-the term "short tons" calls it to my mind-that there is a common practice for the operators to pay the men on the basis of what is known as the long ton or English ton and to sell the goods on the basis of the short ton oi American ton-again a very unfair thing Surely if we have standards of any kind in this country which must be adhered to, we ought to have a standard of measurement in regard to coal.
We have at the present time in the province of Alberta a commission sitting on this whole question of the operation of the coal mines in that province. Their findings, ol course, are not yet available, and failing these I would like to quote a few sentences from a report with regard to the coal mining industry of the province of Alberta made as early as 1919, which indicates pretty much the difficulties that confront the miners in that area. It says:
Many mines only operate one-half of the year or less. If more continuous operation is obtained, the result will be a reduction in the price of coal to the consumer and steadier employment to the workman.

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
Again:
Provisions for making working agreements, the settling of disputes and such matters that employer and employee deal with, are not satisfactory.
Again:
At many mines the living and housing conditions, and matters pertaining to health and sanitation, are not in a satisfactory condition.
Again:
In some camps the educational facilities are inadequate.
Again:
Much capital expenditure has been lost on account of failure to obtain reliable information about properties and marketing conditions before operations are commenced; and also owing to lack of sufficient capital being provided to carry on operations to a successful issue.
Again:
A considerable loss of market has been sustained owing to: cessations of work; shortage of railway cars; misrepresentation as to size and quality of coal.
Still again:
Your commissioners are of the opinion that considerable saving would be attained if owners would establish some central purchasing agency, thereby standardizing equipment; also that a considerable saving would be attained if the power used were obtained from central powei plants located in the various fields. The carrying out of these suggestions, in the opinion of your commissioners, would decrease the cost price of coal, and would not only be a saving to the consumer, but, in addition, would tend to increase the market. As this province has within its borders the largest known coal resources in the world, the conservation of this heritage should be zealously guarded. Your commissioners therefore recommend that you obtain authority from the federal government for the same commission to be given full powers for the safeguarding of this national asset.
So much for the industry. Now let me turn for a few moments to what the miners think about their present situation. I should gladly have brought this matter to the attention of the House at an earlier date, but owing to our rules of order it has been impossible to do so, and I have felt that I could not pass the first opportunity of giving to the House and to the country some little idea of the almost desperate situation that prevails among the miners in Alberta. As early as March 2 of this year I received the following telegram:
Members and families destitue-credit cut off-many not worked since March 19, 1924-remainder only a few days during eleven months. The agreement consummated October 18, yet operators attempting further reductions and open shop conditions. Want to know if federal government will make some effort to solve this problem.
I have been sent a large number of the actual pay sheets of the company. A study of these sheets-which I shall not take the trouble to read to the House-clearly shows 148i
that the stories which have been told about exorbitant wages being paid are absolutely fairy tales. It may be true that in a few instances contract miners under very favourable conditions earned large wages, but they are unemployed for a very considerable portion of the year. Then my correspondent said on March 12:
This company-the Hillcrest Collieries Limited-in ordinary times employ about four hundred men, with an abundance of petty bosses, including three general managers, also a managing director. Its financial yearly report showed enormous profits in 1924.
Again let me read a communication which I received! from Nordegg on February 23:
The unemployed situation in District 18 is very bad. In Nordegg alone 150 men are unemployed and 400 men on two days a week. Poverty and suffering through lack of clothes and food in this cold region is much in evidence.
A few days ago I had this further communication from the same district and from the same writer, and I would ask the House to pay careful1 consideration to it:
There are within this province ten thousand unemployed, and the miners of Alberta wbo are working are not earning enough to keep themselves owing to the company keeping the pay for strike rent; there is much poverty and destitution, and no help from anywhere; women and children starving; and the coal operators taking advantage of the situation and violating the agreement arrived at between District 18 and the Western Canada Coal Operators Association.
Listen to this:
We have exhausted all methods within the law of the country. We have adopted Murdock's method of going " to the foot of the throne." Nothing has been overlooked to try and get some food and clothes in full accord with the law, but every time we have been met with the same answer of No. Now for the last time we are asking the government, through you, to bring in some measures whereby the people of this country can eat. We do not want to take the law into our own hands, but the women and children have to be fed. Therefore on behalf of the five hundred organized workers of Nordegg, and in the interests of the starving people of Alberta, I ask you to try and get something for our fellow beings. The whole situation is more serious than is realized by the King government and the opposition in the House.
We have been told, Mr. Speaker, by tlhe Minister of Labour and by the government that Nova Scotia owns the coal mines of the province; we have been told that Nova Scotia receives royalties on every ton of coal taken from those mines; we have been told that Nova Scotia leases the coal mines to the British Empire Steel Corporation. I want to point out that in Alberta it is the Dominion government that leases the coal mines, it is the Dominion government that receives the royalties, and I should like to ask the Minister of Labour-I am sorry he is not in his seat- ivhat excuse he is going to find now for inaction?

One or two quotations only from the miners' standpoint, and I am done. I want to emphasize that to-night I am trying to place before this House what has not frequently been placed before it, that is, the position of the actual working miners in Canada.	The
secretary of the United Mine Workers of America makes this statement on March 30:
You will find enclosed herewith miner's family budget of prices compiled from information received from various mining camps in District No. 18, which you will readily see is far in excess of the earnings of the miners in this district. The average number of days worked in District No. 18 for the past three years have been 125. Contract miner's average rate, according to the Labour Gazette from the Department of Labour, Ottawa, was $9.08 per shift, making a total for 125 days of $1,135. All day wage labour average earnings, inside and outside the mine, are $6.89, making a total for 125 days of $1,040. On October 10, 1924, the miners suffered a reduction of 12J per cent, which by combining the average earnings of contract miners and day wage rates together, would show the average earnings of the miners throughout District No. 18 at $958.
The family budget issued by the Department of Labour is taken from five cities in the province of Alberta, namely, Calgary, Edmonton, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat and Drumheller. The average is $21.09 per week for a family of five, making a total for 52 weeks of $1,082.12. This budget does not include clothing and sundries, so it is evident that the budget issued by the Department of Labour is far below the one I am enclosing, which was taken from the cost of these items in the camps in District No. 18, and according to that budget we have a total, including clothing and other items, of $1,865.51.
Now with regard to the proposed alterations in the duties I think it is only fair to read the statement of the United Mine Workers of Alberta. The Minister of National Defence asked1 me a question a little while ago and I should like in reply to him to give the statement of the miners in Alberta:
You will also find enclosed statement of cost of coal transportation from the mines at Pocahontas, West Virginia to Winnipeg and also from Youghiegheny, Pennsylvania, to Winnipeg which averages at $7 per ton, and we are informed by the Secretary of the Western Canada Coal Operators' Association that this coal is being sold at less than the cost of transportation to the consumers at Winnipeg. It is evident to me that this coal is bein^ placed on the market at Winnipeg at this price for the purpose of keeping coal mined in Canada from getting the market in Winnipeg and east of that city. The freight rates from Crcwsnest pass to Winnipeg are $5.20 and the

price of coal f.o.b. at the mine is $4.50 making a total of $9.70 per ton sold in Winnipeg, so you will readily see that it is impossible for the Operators of District No. 18 to compete against the American coal now being shipped into Winnipeg.
I have one other communication from the miners with regard to this same matter of duty:
The officers and members of District 18 United Mine Workers of America strongly protest against the action of the federal government in revising the duty on bituminous lump coal from the United States to Canada due to the fact that this will cause a further increase in unemployment throughout the mines of District 18.
Now, Mr. Speaker, one more quotation this *time from the president of the United Mine Workers of Alberta. It says:
The Miners' Executive of District No. 18 recognize that the coal industry in the west is in a serious state [DOT] of over-development. This situation has been admitted by the Minister of Labour and also conceded by all those familiar with the affairs of the coal mining industry but in spite of this deplorable condition new corporations are continually developing and opening up coal mines in western Canada. In spite of our appeals to the authorities to take action in the matter this wildcat development still continues with the final and inevitable result of more slack time and unemployment for the miners already settled around the industry. Government action to prevent the further exploiting of the natural resources of the west should be taken without delay if serious developments in the future are to be avoided. The miners are of the opinion that some tribunal should be appointed by the Dominion government and that said tribunal should have the authority to investigate the records and the books with a view of ascertaining the profits of all coal companies in this district. We believe said tribunal should have power to look into every phase of the industry with a view of preventing the further exploitation of the coal fields by various coal operating firms. In fact it appears to the miners that the only complete solution to the difficulty would be a practicable plan of nationalization of the coal mines, said mines to be operated under the direction of practical mining men.
I have pointed out, Mr. Speaker, some of the evils of the existing system of production. We have very heavy overhead expenses; we have numerous officials; we have watered stock; and side by side we have inefficiency. There must of necessity be inefficiency in small scale mining. Anyone who has visited the mines of the west will know that when you have a very small area with a dozen or twenty mines trying to carry on operations you must have inefficiency; in some way they should be organized. We have over-development and let me remind you that it is the Dominion government that is responsible for the granting of these leases to these various companies; and above all we have what is of importance to the workers, and of great importance I should think to the country at large, unemployment. At this late hour, I do not propose to attempt to point out the solu-

Questions
tion. I had hoped that if I could have reached this subject earlier in the session I would have been able to discuss at some length a resolution which I had on the order paper to the following effect:
That, in the opinion of this House, measures should be taken to regain for the use of the people the coal mines which are now being exploited in the interests of private corporations rather than for the needs of the public.
I would simply leave that resolution with the House, suggesting that it is along those lines and along those lines only that we can hope for the solution of these urgent problems which are pressing upon us at the present time.
